entries.fa35a0aee047150397e8e1cc2a25cbeffa79bbd2: <div sID="gen10642" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="18" osisID="Ps.18" sID="Ps.18"/> <div eID="gen10642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10643" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10644" type="x-p"/> This psalm we met with before, in the history of David's life, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.1-2Sam.22.51">2 Sam. xxii.</reference> That was the first edition of it; here we have it revived, altered a little, and fitted for the service of the church. It is David's thanksgiving for the many deliverances God had wrought for him; these he desired always to preserve fresh in his own memory and to diffuse and entail the knowledge of them. It is an admirable composition. The poetry is very fine, the images are bold, the expressions lofty, and every word is proper and significant; but the piety far exceeds the poetry. Holy faith, and love, and joy, and praise, and hope, are here lively, active, and upon the wing. I. He triumphs in God, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.1-Ps.18.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. He magnifies the deliverances God had wrought for him, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.4-Ps.18.19">ver. 4-19</reference>. III. He takes the comfort of his integrity, which God had thereby cleared up, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.20-Ps.18.28">ver. 20-28</reference>. IV. He gives to God the glory of all his achievements, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.29-Ps.18.42">ver. 29-42</reference>. V. He encourages himself with the expectation of what God would further do for him and his, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.43-Ps.18.50">ver. 43-50</reference>.
entries.fdbd7e83dac3b5605ec680684c4a8313b6e08396: <div eID="gen10644" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10643" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Triumphs in God; Devout Confidence.</title> <div sID="gen10645" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I will love thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , my strength. <hi type="super">2</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, <hi type="italic">and</hi> my high tower. <hi type="super">3</hi> I will call upon the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">who is worthy</hi> to be praised: so shall I be saved from mine enemies. 4 The sorrows of death compassed me, and the floods of ungodly men made me afraid. <hi type="super">5</hi> The sorrows of hell compassed me about: the snares of death prevented me. <hi type="super">6</hi> In my distress I called upon the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and cried unto my God: he heard my voice out of his temple, and my cry came before him, <hi type="italic">even</hi> into his ears. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then the earth shook and trembled; the foundations also of the hills moved and were shaken, because he was wroth. <hi type="super">8</hi> There went up a smoke out of his nostrils, and fire out of his mouth devoured: coals were kindled by it. <hi type="super">9</hi> He bowed the heavens also, and came down: and darkness <hi type="italic">was</hi> under his feet. <hi type="super">10</hi> And he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: yea, he did fly upon the wings of the wind. 11 He made darkness his secret place; his pavilion round about him <hi type="italic">were</hi> dark waters <hi type="italic">and</hi> thick clouds of the skies. <hi type="super">12</hi> At the brightness <hi type="italic">that was</hi> before him his thick clouds passed, hail <hi type="italic">stones</hi> and coals of fire. <hi type="super">13</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> also thundered in the heavens, and the Highest gave his voice; hail <hi type="italic">stones</hi> and coals of fire. <hi type="super">14</hi> Yea, he sent out his arrows, and scattered them; and he shot out lightnings, and discomfited them. <hi type="super">15</hi> Then the channels of waters were seen, and the foundations of the world were discovered at thy rebuke, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , at the blast of the breath of thy nostrils. <hi type="super">16</hi> He sent from above, he took me, he drew me out of many waters. 17 He delivered me from my strong enemy, and from them which hated me: for they were too strong for me. <hi type="super">18</hi> They prevented me in the day of my calamity: but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was my stay. <hi type="super">19</hi> He brought me forth also into a large place; he delivered me, because he delighted in me. <div eID="gen10645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10646" type="x-p"/> The title gives us the occasion of penning this psalm; we had it before (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.1">2 Sam. xxii. 1</reference>), only here we are told that the psalm was delivered <hi type="italic">to the chief musician,</hi> or precentor, in the temple-songs. Note, The private compositions of good men, designed by them for their own use, may be serviceable to the public, that others may not only borrow light from their candle, but heat from their fire. Examples sometimes teach better than rules. And David is here called <hi type="italic">the servant of the Lord,</hi> as Moses was, not only as every good man is God's servant, but because, with his sceptre, with his sword, and with his pen, he greatly promoted the interests of God's kingdom in Israel. It was more his honour that he was a servant of the Lord than that he was king of a great kingdom; and so he himself accounted it (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.16">Ps. cxvi. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">O Lord! truly I am thy servant.</hi> In these verses, <div eID="gen10646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10647" type="x-p"/> I. He triumphs in God and his relation to him. The first words of the psalm, <hi type="italic">I will love thee, O Lord! my strength,</hi> are here prefixed as the scope and contents of the whole. Love to God is the first and great commandment of the law, because it is the principle of all our acceptable praise and obedience; and this use we should make of all the mercies God bestows upon us, our hearts should thereby be enlarged in love to him. This he requires and will accept; and we are very ungrateful if we grudge him so poor a return. An interest in the person loved is the lover's delight; this string therefore he touches, and on this he harps with much pleasure (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The Lord</hi> Jehovah <hi type="italic">is my</hi> God; and then he is my <hi type="italic">rock, my fortress,</hi> all that I need and can desire in my present distress." For there is that in God which is suited to all the exigencies and occasions of his people that trust in him. "He is my rock, and strength, and fortress;" that is, 1. "I have found him so in the greatest dangers and difficulties." 2. "I have chosen him to be so, disclaiming all others, and depending upon him alone to protect me." Those that truly love God may thus triumph in him as theirs, and may with confidence call upon him, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.3">v. 3</reference>. This further use we should make of our deliverances, we must not only love God the better, but love prayer the better—<hi type="italic">call upon him as long as we live,</hi> especially in time of trouble, with an assurance that so we shall be saved; for thus it is written, <hi type="italic">Whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.21">Acts ii. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen10647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10648" type="x-p"/> II. He sets himself to magnify the deliverances God had wrought for him, that he might be the more affected in his returns of praise. It is good for us to observe all the circumstances of a mercy, which magnify the power of God and his goodness to us in it. <div eID="gen10648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10649" type="x-p"/> 1. The more imminent and threatening the danger was out of which we were delivered the greater is the mercy of the deliverance. David now remembered how the forces of his enemies poured in upon him, which he calls <hi type="italic">the floods of Belial,</hi> shoals of the children of Belial, likely to overpower him with numbers. They surrounded him, <hi type="italic">compassed him about;</hi> they surprised him, and by that means were very near seizing him; their snares prevented him, and, when without were fightings, within were fears and sorrows, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.4-Ps.18.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. His spirit was overwhelmed, and he looked upon himself as a lost man; see <reference osisRef="Ps.116.3">Ps. cxvi. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen10649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10650" type="x-p"/> 2. The more earnest we have been with God for deliverance, and the more direct answer it is to our prayers, the more we are obliged to be thankful. David's deliverances were so, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.6">v. 6</reference>. David was found a praying man, and God was found a prayer-hearing God. If we pray as he did, we shall speed as he did. Though distress drive us to prayer, God will not therefore be deaf to us; nay, being a God of pity, he will be the more ready to succour us. <div eID="gen10650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10651" type="x-p"/> 3. The more wonderful God's appearances are in any deliverance the greater it is: such were the deliverances wrought for David, in which God's manifestation of his presence and glorious attributes is most magnificently described, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.7-Ps.18.15">v. 7</reference>, &c. Little appeared of man, but much of God, in these deliverances. (1.) He appeared a God of almighty power; for he made the earth shake and tremble, and moved even the <hi type="italic">foundations of the hills</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.7">v. 7</reference>), as of old at Mount Sinai. When the men of the earth were struck with fear, then the earth might be said to <hi type="italic">tremble;</hi> when the great men of the earth were put into confusion, then the hills moved. (2.) He showed his anger and displeasure against the enemies and persecutors of his people: <hi type="italic">He was wroth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.7">v. 7</reference>. His wrath smoked, it burned, it was fire, it was devouring fire (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.8">v. 8</reference>), and <hi type="italic">coals were kindled by it.</hi> Those that by their own sins make themselves as coals (that is, fuel) to this fire will be consumed by it. He that ordains his arrows against the persecutors sends them forth when he pleases, and they are sure to hit the mark and do execution; for those arrows are lightnings, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.14">v. 14</reference>. (3.) He showed his readiness to plead his people's cause and work deliverance for them; for he rode upon a cherub and did fly, for the maintaining of right and the relieving of his distressed servants, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.10">v. 10</reference>. No opposition, no obstruction, can be given to him <hi type="italic">who rides upon the wings of the wind, who rides on the heavens, for the help of his people, and, in his excellency, on the skies.</hi> (4.) He showed his condescension, in taking cognizance of David's case: <hi type="italic">He bowed the heavens and came down</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.9">v. 9</reference>), did not send an angel, but came himself, as one afflicted in the afflictions of his people. (5.) He wrapped himself in darkness, and yet commanded light to shine out of darkness for his people, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.15">Isa. xlv. 15</reference>. He is a God that hideth himself; for he <hi type="italic">made darkness his pavilion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.11">v. 11</reference>. his glory is invisible, his counsels are unsearchable, and his proceedings unaccountable, and so, as to us, clouds and darkness are round about him; we know not the way that he takes, even when he is coming towards us in ways of mercy; but, when his designs are secret, they are kind; for, though he hide himself, he is the God of Israel, the Saviour. And, <hi type="italic">at his brightness, the thick clouds pass</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.12">v. 12</reference>), comfort returns, the face of affairs is changed, and that which was gloomy and threatening becomes serene and pleasant. <div eID="gen10651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10652" type="x-p"/> 4. The greater the difficulties are that lie in the way of deliverance the more glorious the deliverance is. For the rescuing of David, the waters were to be divided till the very channels were seen; the earth was to be cloven till the very foundations of it were discovered, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.15">v. 15</reference>. There were waters deep and many, waters out of which he was to be drawn (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.16">v. 16</reference>), as Moses, who had his name from being drawn out of the water literally, as David was figuratively. His enemies were strong, and they hated him; had he been left to himself, they would have been too strong for him, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.17">v. 17</reference>. And they were too quick for him; for they <hi type="italic">prevented him in the day of his calamity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.18">v. 18</reference>. But, in the midst of his troubles, the Lord was his stay, so that he did not sink. Note, God will not only deliver his people out of their troubles in due time, but he will sustain them and bear them up under their troubles in the mean time. <div eID="gen10652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10653" type="x-p"/> 5. That which especially magnified the deliverance was that his comfort was the fruit of it and God's favour was the root and fountain of it. (1.) It was an introduction to his preferment, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.19">v. 19</reference>. "He brought me forth also out of my straits into a large place, where I had room, not only to turn, but to thrive in." (2.) It was a token of God's favour to him, and that made it doubly sweet: "<hi type="italic">He delivered me because he delighted in me,</hi> not for my merit, but for his own grace and good-will." Compare this with <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.26">2 Sam. xv. 26</reference>, <hi type="italic">If he thus say, I have no delight in thee, here I am.</hi> We owe our salvation, that great deliverance, to the delight God had in the Son of David, in whom he has declared himself to be well pleased. <div eID="gen10653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10654" type="x-p"/> In singing this we must triumph in God, and trust in him: and we may apply it to Christ the Son of David. The sorrows of death surrounded him; in his distress he prayed (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>); God made the earth to shake and tremble, and the rocks to cleave, and brought him out, in his resurrection, into a large place, because he delighted in him and in his undertaking.
entries.0690c96bd9c7936dbf1d1702b8393ffd5030df47: <div eID="gen10654" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Devout Thanksgivings; Devout Confidence</title> <div sID="gen10655" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> rewarded me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands hath he recompensed me. <hi type="super">21</hi> For I have kept the ways of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and have not wickedly departed from my God. <hi type="super">22</hi> For all his judgments <hi type="italic">were</hi> before me, and I did not put away his statutes from me. 23 I was also upright before him, and I kept myself from mine iniquity. <hi type="super">24</hi> Therefore hath the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> recompensed me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands in his eyesight. <hi type="super">25</hi> With the merciful thou wilt show thyself merciful; with an upright man thou wilt show thyself upright; 26 With the pure thou wilt show thyself pure; and with the froward thou wilt show thyself froward. <hi type="super">27</hi> For thou wilt save the afflicted people; but wilt bring down high looks. <hi type="super">28</hi> For thou wilt light my candle: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> my God will enlighten my darkness. <div eID="gen10655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10656" type="x-p"/> Here, I. David reflects with comfort upon his own integrity, and rejoices in the testimony of his conscience that he had had his conversation in godly sincerity and not with fleshly wisdom, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12">2 Cor. i. 12</reference>. His deliverances were an evidence of this, and this was the great comfort of his deliverances. His enemies had misrepresented him, and perhaps, when his troubles continued long, he began to suspect himself; but, when God visibly took his part, he had both the credit and the comfort of his righteousness. 1. His deliverances cleared his innocency before men, and acquitted him from those crimes which he was falsely accused of. This he calls <hi type="italic">rewarding him according to his righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.20">v. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.24">24</reference>), that is, determining the controversy between him and his enemies, according to the justice of his cause and the cleanness of his hands, from that sedition, treason, and rebellion, with which he was charged. He had often appealed to God concerning his innocency; and now God had given judgment upon the appeal (as he always will) according to equity. 2. They confirmed the testimony of his own conscience for him, which he here reviews with a great deal of pleasure, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.21-Ps.18.23">v. 21-23</reference>. His own heart knows, and is ready to attest it, (1.) That he had kept firmly to his duty, and had not departed, not wickedly, not wilfully departed, from his God. Those that forsake the ways of the Lord do, in effect, depart from their God, and it is a wicked thing to do so. But though we are conscious to ourselves of many a stumble, and many a false step taken, yet if we recover ourselves by repentance, and go on in the way of our duty, it shall not be construed into a departure, for it is not a wicked departure, from our God. (2.) That he had kept his eye upon the rule of God's commands (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.22">v. 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">All his judgments were before me;</hi> and I had a respect to them all, despised none as little, disliked none as hard, but made it my care and business to conform to them all. His statutes I did not put away from me, out of my sight, out of my mind, but kept my eye always upon them, and did not as those who, because they would quit the ways of the Lord, desire not the knowledge of those ways." (3.) That he had kept himself from his iniquity, and thereby had approved himself upright before God. Constant care to abstain from that sin, whatever it be, which most easily besets us, and to mortify the habit of it, will be a good evidence for us that we are upright before God. As David's deliverances cleared his integrity, so did the exaltation of Christ clear his, and for ever roll away the reproach that was cast upon him; and therefore he is said to be <hi type="italic">justified in the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1 Tim. iii. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen10656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10657" type="x-p"/> II. He takes occasion thence to lay down the rules of God's government and judgment, that we may know not only what God expects from us, but what we may expect from him, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.25-Ps.18.26">v. 25, 26</reference>. 1. Those that show mercy to others (even they need mercy, and cannot depend upon the merit, no, not of their works of mercy) shall find mercy with God, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.7">Matt. v. 7</reference>. 2. Those that are faithful to their covenants with God, and the relations wherein they stand to him, shall find him all that to them which he has promised to be. Wherever God finds an upright man, he will be found an upright God. 3. Those that serve God with a pure conscience shall find that the words of the Lord are pure words, very sure to be depended on and very sweet to be delighted in. 4. Those that resist God, and walk contrary to him, shall find that he will resist them, and walk contrary to them, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.21">Lev. xxvi. 21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.24">24</reference>. <div eID="gen10657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10658" type="x-p"/> III. Hence he speaks comfort to the humble ("<hi type="italic">Thou wilt save the afflicted people,</hi> that are wronged and bear it patiently"), terror to the proud ("Thou <hi type="italic">wilt bring down high looks,</hi> that aim high, and look with scorn and disdain upon the poor and pious"), and encouragement to himself—"<hi type="italic">Thou wilt light my candle,</hi> that is, thou wilt revive and comfort my sorrowful spirit, and not leave me melancholy; thou wilt recover me out of my troubles and restore me to peace and prosperity; thou wilt make my honour bright, which is now eclipsed; thou wilt guide my way, and make it plain before me, that I may avoid the snares laid for me; thou wilt light my candle to work by, and give me an opportunity of serving thee and the interests of thy kingdom among men." <div eID="gen10658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10659" type="x-p"/> Let those that walk in darkness, and labour under many discouragements in singing these verses, encourage themselves that God himself will be a light to them.
entries.1c10234b6e3b41434a3f72f353fdb0f70b60775e: <div eID="gen10659" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Grateful Remembrance of Past Deliverances; Confidence in the Divine Goodness.</title> <div sID="gen10660" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> For by thee I have run through a troop; and by my God have I leaped over a wall. <hi type="super">30</hi> <hi type="italic">As for</hi> God, his way <hi type="italic">is</hi> perfect: the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> is tried: he <hi type="italic">is</hi> a buckler to all those that trust in him. <hi type="super">31</hi> For who <hi type="italic">is</hi> God save the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? or who <hi type="italic">is</hi> a rock save our God? <hi type="super">32</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> God that girdeth me with strength, and maketh my way perfect. <hi type="super">33</hi> He maketh my feet like hinds' <hi type="italic">feet,</hi> and setteth me upon my high places. <hi type="super">34</hi> He teacheth my hands to war, so that a bow of steel is broken by mine arms. <hi type="super">35</hi> Thou hast also given me the shield of thy salvation: and thy right hand hath holden me up, and thy gentleness hath made me great. <hi type="super">36</hi> Thou hast enlarged my steps under me, that my feet did not slip. <hi type="super">37</hi> I have pursued mine enemies, and overtaken them: neither did I turn again till they were consumed. <hi type="super">38</hi> I have wounded them that they were not able to rise: they are fallen under my feet. <hi type="super">39</hi> For thou hast girded me with strength unto the battle: thou hast subdued under me those that rose up against me. <hi type="super">40</hi> Thou hast also given me the necks of mine enemies; that I might destroy them that hate me. 41 They cried, but <hi type="italic">there was</hi> none to save <hi type="italic">them: even</hi> unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , but he answered them not. <hi type="super">42</hi> Then did I beat them small as the dust before the wind: I did cast them out as the dirt in the streets. 43 Thou hast delivered me from the strivings of the people; <hi type="italic">and</hi> thou hast made me the head of the heathen: a people <hi type="italic">whom</hi> I have not known shall serve me. <hi type="super">44</hi> As soon as they hear of me, they shall obey me: the strangers shall submit themselves unto me. <hi type="super">45</hi> The strangers shall fade away, and be afraid out of their close places. <hi type="super">46</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth; and blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> my rock; and let the God of my salvation be exalted. <hi type="super">47</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> God that avengeth me, and subdueth the people under me. <hi type="super">48</hi> He delivereth me from mine enemies: yea, thou liftest me up above those that rise up against me: thou hast delivered me from the violent man. <hi type="super">49</hi> Therefore will I give thanks unto thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , among the heathen, and sing praises unto thy name. <hi type="super">50</hi> Great deliverance giveth he to his king; and showeth mercy to his anointed, to David, and to his seed for evermore. <div eID="gen10660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10661" type="x-p"/> In these verses, <div eID="gen10661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10662" type="x-p"/> I. David looks back, with thankfulness, upon the great things which God had done for him. He had not only wrought deliverance for him, but had given him victory and success, and made him triumph over those who thought to triumph over him. When we set ourselves to praise God for one mercy we must be led by that to observe the many more with which we have been compassed about, and followed, all our days. Many things had contributed to David's advancement, and he owns the hand of God in them all, to teach us to do likewise, in reviewing the several steps by which we have risen to our prosperity. 1. God had given him all his skill and understanding in military affairs, which he was not bred up to nor designed for, his genius leading him more to music, and poetry, and a contemplative life: <hi type="italic">He teaches my hands to war,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.34">v. 34</reference>. 2. God had given him bodily strength to go through the business and fatigue of war: God <hi type="italic">girded him with strength</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.32">v. 32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.39">39</reference>), to such a degree that he could break even a bow of steel, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.34">v. 34</reference>. What service God designs men for he will be sure to fit them for. 3. God had likewise given him great swiftness, not to flee from the enemies but to fly upon them (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">He makes my feet like hinds' feet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.36">v. 36</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Thou hast enlarged my steps under me;</hi> but" (whereas those that take large steps are apt to tread awry) "my feet did not slip." He was so swift that he pursued his enemies and overtook them, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.37">v. 37</reference>. 4. God had made him very bold and daring in his enterprises, and given him spirit proportionable to his strength. If a troop stood in his way, he made nothing of running through them; if a wall, he made nothing of leaping over it (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.29">v. 29</reference>); if ramparts and bulwarks, he soon mounted them, and by divine assistance set his feet upon the high places of the enemy, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.33">v. 33</reference>. 5. God had protected him, and kept him safe, in the midst of the greatest perils. Many a time he put his life in his hand, and yet it was wonderfully preserved: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast given me the shield of thy salvation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.35">v. 35</reference>), and that has compassed me on every side. By that I have been delivered from the strivings of the people who aimed at my destruction (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.43">v. 43</reference>), particularly from the violent man" (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.48">v. 48</reference>), that is, Saul, who more than once threw a javelin at him. 6. God had prospered him in his designs; he it was that made his way perfect (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.32">v. 32</reference>) and it was his right hand that held him up, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.35">v. 35</reference>. 7. God had given him victory over his enemies, the Philistines, Moabites, Ammonites, and all that fought against Israel: those especially he means, yet not excluding the house of Saul, which opposed his coming to the crown, and the partisans of Absalom and Sheba, who would have deposed him. He enlarges much upon the goodness of God to him in defeating his enemies, attributing his victories, not to his own sword or bow, nor to the valour of his mighty men, but to the favour of God: <hi type="italic">I pursued</hi> them (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.37">v. 37</reference>), <hi type="italic">I wounded them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.38">v. 38</reference>); <hi type="italic">for thou hast girded me with strength</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.39">v. 39</reference>), else I could not have done it. All the praise is ascribed to God: <hi type="italic">Thou hast subdued them under me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.39">v. 39</reference>. Thou hast <hi type="italic">given me their necks</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.40">v. 40</reference>), not only to trample upon them (as <reference osisRef="Josh.10.24">Josh. x. 24</reference>), but to cut them off. Even those who hated David whom God loved, and were enemies to the Israel of God, in their distress cried unto the Lord: but in vain; he answered them not. How could they expect he should when it was he whom they fought against? And, when he disowned them (as he will all those that act against his people), no other succours could stand them in stead: <hi type="italic">There was none to save them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.41">v. 41</reference>. Those whom God has abandoned are easily vanquished: <hi type="italic">Then did I beat them small as the dust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.42">v. 42</reference>. But those whose cause is just he avenges (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.47">v. 47</reference>), and those whom he favours will certainly be <hi type="italic">lifted up above those that rise up against them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.48">v. 48</reference>. 8. God had raised him to the throne, and not only delivered him and kept him alive, but dignified him and made him great (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy gentleness has increased me</hi>—thy <hi type="italic">discipline</hi> and <hi type="italic">instruction;</hi> so some. The good lessons David learned in his affliction prepared him for the dignity and power that were intended him; and the lessening of him helped very much to increase his greatness. God made him not only a great conqueror, but a great ruler: <hi type="italic">Thou hast made me the head of the heathen</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.43">v. 43</reference>); all the neighbouring nations were tributaries to him. See <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.6">2 Sam. viii. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.11">11</reference>. In all this David was a type of Christ, whom the Father brought safely through his conflicts with the powers of darkness, and made victorious over them, and gave to be head over all things to his church, which is his body. <div eID="gen10662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10663" type="x-p"/> II. David looks up with humble and reverent adorations of the divine glory and perfection. When God had, by his providence, magnified him, he endeavours, with his praises, to magnify God, to bless him and exalt him, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.46">v. 46</reference>. He gives honour to him, 1. As a living God: <hi type="italic">The Lord liveth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.46">v. 46</reference>. We had our lives at first from, and we owe the continuance of them to, that God who has life in himself and is therefore fitly called <hi type="italic">the living God.</hi> The gods of the heathen were dead gods. The best friends we have among men are dying friends. But God lives, lives for ever, and will not fail those that trust in him, but, because he lives, they shall live also; for he is their life. 2. As a finishing God: <hi type="italic">As for God,</hi> he is not only perfect himself, but <hi type="italic">his way is perfect,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.30">v. 30</reference>. He is known by his name <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.3">Exod. vi. 3</reference>), a God performing and perfecting what he begins in providence as well as creation, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.1">Gen. ii. 1</reference>. If it was God that made David's way perfect (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.32">v. 32</reference>), much more is his own way so. There is no flaw in God's works, nor any fault to be found with what he does, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.14">Eccl. iii. 14</reference>. And what he undertakes he will go through with, whatever difficulties lie in the way; what God begins to build he is able to finish. 3. As a faithful God: <hi type="italic">The word of the Lord is tried.</hi> "I have tried it" (says David), "and it has not failed me." All the saints, in all ages, have tried it, and it never failed any that trusted in it. It is tried as silver is tried, refined from all such mixture and alloy as lessen the value of men's words. David, in God's providences concerning him, takes notice of the performance of his promises to him, which, as it puts sweetness into the providence, so it puts honour upon the promise. 4. As the protector and defender of his people. David had found him so to him: "<hi type="italic">He is the God of my salvation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.46">v. 46</reference>), by whose power and grace I am and hope to be saved; but not of mine only: he is <hi type="italic">a buckler to all those that trust in him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.30">v. 30</reference>); he shelters and protects them all, is both able and ready to do so." 5. As a non-such in all this, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.31">v. 31</reference>. There is a God, and <hi type="italic">who is God save Jehovah?</hi> That God is a rock, for the support and shelter of his faithful worshippers; and <hi type="italic">who is a rock save our God?</hi> Thus he not only gives glory to God, but encourages his own faith in him. Note, (1.) Whoever pretends to be deities, it is certain that there is no God, save the Lord; all others are counterfeits, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.8">Isa. xliv. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.10">Jer. x. 10</reference>. (2.) Whoever pretends to be our felicities, there is no rock, save our God; none that we can depend upon to make us happy. <div eID="gen10663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10664" type="x-p"/> III. David looks forward, with a believing hope that God would still do him good. He promises himself, 1. That his enemies should be completely subdued, and that those of them that yet remained should be made his footstool,—that his government should be extensive, so that even a people whom he had not known should serve him (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.43">v. 43</reference>),—that his conquests, and, consequently, his acquests, should be easy (<hi type="italic">As soon as they hear of me they shall obey me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.44">v. 44</reference>), —and that his enemies should be convinced that it was to no purpose to oppose him; even those that had retired to their fastnesses should not trust to them, but be afraid out of their close places, having seen so much of David's wisdom, courage, and success. Thus the Son of David, though he sees not yet all things put under him, yet knows he shall reign till all opposing rule, principality, and power shall be quite put down. 2. That his seed should be forever continued in the Messiah, who, he foresaw, should come from his loins, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.50">v. 50</reference>. He <hi type="italic">shows mercy to his anointed,</hi> his Messiah, <hi type="italic">to David</hi> himself, the anointed of the God of Jacob in the type, <hi type="italic">and to his seed for evermore. He saith not unto seeds, as of many, but to his seed, as of one, that is Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.3.16">Gal. iii. 16</reference>. It is he only that shall reign for ever, and of the increase of whose government and peace there shall be no end. Christ is called <hi type="italic">David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Hos. iii. 5</reference>. God has called him <hi type="italic">his king,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Ps. ii. 6</reference>. Great deliverance God does give, and will give to him, and to his church and people, here called <hi type="italic">his seed, for evermore.</hi> <div eID="gen10664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10665" type="x-p"/> In singing <reference osisRef="Ps.18.29-Ps.18.50">these verses</reference> we must give God the glory of the victories of Christ and his church hitherto and of all the deliverances and advancements of the gospel kingdom, and encourage ourselves and one another with an assurance that the church militant will be shortly triumphant, will be eternally so.  <chapter eID="Ps.18"/> <div eID="gen10665" type="x-p"/>

entries.466613a369999e19b4882d8098e21a17ff3ca32f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5611"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 18</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.18.1-Ps.18.50">Psa 18:1-50</reference>. "The servant of the Lord," which in the Hebrew precedes "David," is a significant part of the title (and not a mere epithet of David), denoting the inspired character of the song, as the production of one entrusted with the execution of God's will. He was not favored by God because he served Him, but served Him because selected and appointed by God in His sovereign mercy. After a general expression of praise and confidence in God for the future, David gives a sublimely poetical description of God's deliverance, which he characterizes as an illustration of God's justice to the innocent and His righteous government. His own prowess and success are celebrated as the results of divine aid, and, confident of its continuance, he closes in terms of triumphant praise. <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.1-2Sam.22.51">2Sa 22:1-51</reference> is a copy of this Psalm, with a few unimportant variations recorded there as a part of the history, and repeated here as part of a collection designed for permanent use.</title> <div sID="gen8539" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5611"/><hi type="bold">1. I will love thee--</hi>with most tender affection. <div eID="gen8539" type="x-p"/>
entries.443a92c49273bb538b755a713f954e366436abca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5612"/><div sID="gen8540" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5612"/>2-3. The various terms used describe God as an object of the most implicit and reliable trust.<div eID="gen8540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rock--</hi>literally, "a cleft rock," for concealment.<div eID="gen8541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8542" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strength--</hi>a firm, immovable rock.<div eID="gen8542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8543" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horn of my salvation--</hi>The horn, as the means of attack or defense of some of the strongest animals, is a frequent emblem of power or strength efficiently exercised (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.33.17">De 33:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.69">Lu 1:69</reference>).<div eID="gen8543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8544" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tower--</hi>literally, "high place," beyond reach of danger. <div eID="gen8544" type="x-p"/>
entries.3955b96595c7a5bca6a9e176a93b661b81a9bdd5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5614"/><div sID="gen8546" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5614"/><hi type="bold">4. sorrows--</hi>literally, "bands as of a net" (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.3">Psa 116:3</reference>).<div eID="gen8546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8547" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">floods--</hi>denotes "multitude." <div eID="gen8547" type="x-p"/>

entries.ffe894d53351e722d41728bd37d90058cd65504a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5625"/><div sID="gen8562" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5625"/>15. entries.c038a3036a3069c9f2483fce23403b034f088e48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5626"/><div sID="gen8563" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5626"/><hi type="bold">16-19. from above--</hi>As seated on a throne, directing these terrible scenes, God--<div eID="gen8563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8564" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sent--</hi>His hand (<reference osisRef="Ps.144.7">Psa 144:7</reference>), reached down to His humble worshipper, and delivered him.<div eID="gen8564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8565" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">many waters--</hi>calamities (<reference osisRef="Job.30.14">Job 30:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.124.4">Psa 124:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.124.5">5</reference>). <div eID="gen8565" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d37eff379e0edc977e3c1d67e870695d964e59f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5629"/><div sID="gen8568" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5629"/>20-24. entries.2ca5fb54dfcce09af29ad71c62609cb3e99de1c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5631"/><div sID="gen8571" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5631"/>25-27. God renders to men according to their deeds in a penal, not vindictive, sense (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.23">Le 26:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.24">24</reference>).<div eID="gen8571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">merciful--</hi>or, "kind" (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Psa 4:3</reference>). <div eID="gen8572" type="x-p"/>
entries.23d6a254b0b9c1adf4ea0c4d7f1eeced43f95ac5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5634"/><div sID="gen8576" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5634"/>28. entries.47fdc6bbd1c64153d01ee033c80ed47b59d8174d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5635"/><div sID="gen8578" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5635"/>29. And this on past experience in his military life, set forth by these figures. <div eID="gen8578" type="x-p"/>
entries.275d44f36b9d90d7e41a9774def35a8a1ae4da34: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5636"/><div sID="gen8579" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5636"/>30-32. God's perfection is the source of his own, which has resulted from his trust on the one hand, and God's promised help on the other.<div eID="gen8579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8580" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tried--</hi>"as metals are tried by fire and proved genuine" (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.6">Psa 12:6</reference>). Shield (<reference osisRef="Ps.3.3">Psa 3:3</reference>). Girding was essential to free motion on account of the looseness of Oriental dresses; hence it is an expressive figure for describing the gift of strength. <div eID="gen8580" type="x-p"/>
entries.e514839eb54820cbca343d1e434714e80d253abb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5637"/><div sID="gen8581" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5637"/>33-36. entries.921dd56205776d7ca9007c10e3cfd9efd878b9b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5640"/><div sID="gen8584" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5640"/>37-41. entries.205bf09ac72b3148e15d5e06643bafc525003456: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5643"/><div sID="gen8587" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5643"/>42. This conquest was complete. <div eID="gen8587" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4fd8fc249221f82cf1348838aff522630cbcb57: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5644"/><div sID="gen8588" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5644"/>43-45. entries.cea596c745aa7756b533e62c7ea046496b8b9d0e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5646"/><div sID="gen8590" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5646"/><hi type="bold">46. The Lord liveth--</hi>contrasts Him with idols (<reference osisRef="1Cor.8.4">1Co 8:4</reference>). <div eID="gen8590" type="x-p"/>
entries.991f735a8d8dc84232978fdcd5ba83fa128d1183: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5647"/><div sID="gen8591" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5647"/><hi type="bold">47-48. avengeth me--</hi>His cause is espoused by God as His own. <div eID="gen8591" type="x-p"/>
entries.349ba6bb4bdfb07ad484acb86727cfab718298e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5649"/><div sID="gen8593" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5649"/>49-50. Paul (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.9">Ro 15:9</reference>) quotes from this doxology to show that under the Old Testament economy, others than the Jews were regarded as subjects of that spiritual government of which David was head, and in which character his deliverances and victories were typical of the more illustrious triumphs of David's greater Son. The language of <reference osisRef="Ps.18.50">Psa 18:50</reference> justifies this view in its distinct allusion to the great promise (compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.12">2Sa 7:12</reference>). In all David's successes he saw the pledges of a fulfilment of that promise, and he mourned in all his adversities, not only in view of his personal suffering, but because he saw in them evidences of danger to the great interests which were committed to his keeping. It is in these aspects of his character that we are led properly to appreciate the importance attached to his sorrows and sufferings, his joys and successes. <chapter eID="Ps.18"/>

entries.bd2b03642df7fe0282dffb86e51a1b9239a6a2c7: <div eID="gen18961" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen18962" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18963" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18963" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18962" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18964" type="x-p"/> David's address of thanks to Jehovah, <reference osisRef="Psa.18.1-Psa.18.3">Psa 18:1-3</reference>. A relation of sufferings undergone, and prayers made for assistance, <reference osisRef="Psa.18.4-Psa.18.6">Psa 18:4-6</reference>. A magnificent description of Divine interposition in behalf of the sufferer, <reference osisRef="Psa.18.7-Psa.18.15">Psa 18:7-15</reference>; and of the deliverance wrought for him, <reference osisRef="Psa.18.16-Psa.18.19">Psa 18:16-19</reference>. That this deliverance was in consideration of his righteousness, <reference osisRef="Psa.18.20-Psa.18.24">Psa 18:20-24</reference>; and according to the tenor of God's equitable proceedings, <reference osisRef="Psa.18.25-Psa.18.28">Psa 18:25-28</reference>. To Jehovah is ascribed the glory of the victory, <reference osisRef="Psa.18.29-Psa.18.36">Psa 18:29-36</reference>; which ts represented as complete by the destruction of all his opponents, <reference osisRef="Psa.18.37-Psa.18.42">Psa 18:37-42</reference>. On these events the heathen submit, <reference osisRef="Psa.18.43-Psa.18.45">Psa 18:43-45</reference>. And for all these things God is glorified, <reference osisRef="Psa.18.46-Psa.18.50">Psa 18:46-50</reference>. <div eID="gen18964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18965" type="x-p"/> The title: "To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David, the servant of the Lord, who spake unto the Lord the words of this song in the day that the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul." <div eID="gen18965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18966" type="x-p"/> Except the first clause, this title is taken from <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.1">2Sam 22:1</reference>. The reader is requested to turn to the notes on <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.1">2Sam 22:1</reference>, for some curious information on this Psalm, particularly what is extracted from Dr. Kennicott. This learned writer supposes the whole to be a song of the Messiah, and divides it into five parts, which he thus introduces: - "The Messiah's sublime thanksgivings, composed by David when his wars were at an end, towards the conclusion of his life. And in this sacred song the goodness of God is celebrated, <div eID="gen18966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18967" type="x-p"/> 1. For Messiah's resurrection from the dead, with the wonders attending that awful event, and soon following it. <div eID="gen18967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18968" type="x-p"/> 2. For the punishment inflicted on the Jews; particularly by the destruction of Jerusalem. And, <div eID="gen18968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18969" type="x-p"/> 3. For the obedience of the Gentile nations. See <reference osisRef="Rom.15.9">Rom 15:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.13">Heb 2:13</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Mat.28.2-Mat.28.4">Mat 28:2-4</reference>; with <reference osisRef="Mat.24.7">Mat 24:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.24.29">Mat 24:29</reference>." <div eID="gen18969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18970" type="x-p"/> And that the title now prefixed to this hymn here and in <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.1">2Sam 22:1</reference>, describes only the time of its composition, seems evident; for who can ascribe to David himself as the subject, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.5">2Sam 22:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.6">2Sam 22:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.8-2Sam.22.17">2Sam 22:8-17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.21-2Sam.22.26">2Sam 22:21-26</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.30">2Sam 22:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.42">2Sam 22:42</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.44">2Sam 22:44</reference>, etc.? <div eID="gen18970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18971" type="x-p"/> In Dr. Kennicott's remarks there is a new translation of the whole Psalm, p. 178, etc. <div eID="gen18971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18972" type="x-p"/> The strong current of commentators and critics apply this Psalm to Christ; and to oppose a whole host of both ancients and moderns would argue great self-confidence. In the main I am of the same mind; and on this principle chiefly I shall proceed to its illustration; still however considering that there are many things in it which concern David, and him only. Drs. Chandler and Delaney have been very successful in their illustration of various passages in it; all the best critics have brought their strongest powers to bear on it; and most of the commentators have labored it with great success; and Bishop Horne has applied the whole of it to Christ. My old Psalter speaks highly in its praise: "This Psalme contenes the sacrement of al chosyn men, the qwilk doand the law of God thurgh the seven fald grace of the Haly Gast fra al temptaciouns, and the pouste of dede and of the devel lesid: this sang thai syng til God; and thankes him and says, I sal luf the Lord, noght a day or twa, bot ever mare: my strength, thurgh quam I am stalworth in thoght." <div eID="gen18972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18973" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen18973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18974" type="x-p"/> I will love thee - Love always subsists on motive and reason. The verb רחם racham signifies to love with all the tender feelinys of nature. "From my inmost bowels will I love thee, O Lord!" Why should he love Jehovah? Not merely because he was infinitely great and good, possessed of all possible perfections, but because he was good to him: and he here enumerates some of the many blessings he received from him. <div eID="gen18974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18975" type="x-p"/> My strength - <div eID="gen18975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18976" type="x-p"/> 1. Thou who hast given me power over my adversaries, and hast enabled me to avoid evil and do good.
entries.ec0b3946cc93f860c68214808d7566a7b756f38d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen18976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18977" type="x-p"/> The Lord is my rock - <div eID="gen18977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18978" type="x-p"/> 2. I stand on him as my foundation, and derive every good from him who is the source of good. The word סלע sela signifies those craggy precipices which afford shelter to men and wild animals; where the bees often made their nests, and whence honey was collected in great abundance. "He made him to suck honey out of the rock," <reference osisRef="Deu.32.13">Deu 32:13</reference>. <div eID="gen18978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18979" type="x-p"/> 3. He was his fortress; a place of strength and safety, fortified by nature and art, where he could be safe from his enemies. He refers to those inaccessible heights in the rocky, mountainous country of Judea, where he had often found refuge from the pursuit of Saul. What these have been to my body, such has the Lord been to my soul. <div eID="gen18979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18980" type="x-p"/> Deliverer - <div eID="gen18980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18981" type="x-p"/> 4. מפלתי mephalleti, he who causes me to escape. This refers to his preservation in straits and difficulties. He was often almost surrounded and taken, but still the Lord made a way for his escape - made a way out as his enemies got in; so that, while they got in at one side of his strong hold, he got out of the other, and so escaped with his life. These escapes were so narrow and so unlikely that he plainly saw the hand of the Lord was in them. <div eID="gen18981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18982" type="x-p"/> 5. My God, אלי ,doG Eli, my strong God, not only the object of my adoration, but he who puts strength in my soul. <div eID="gen18982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18983" type="x-p"/> 6. My strength, צורי tsuri. This is a different word from that in the first verse. <div eID="gen18983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18984" type="x-p"/> Rabbi Maimon has observed that צור tsur, when applied to God, signifies fountain, source, origin, etc. God is not only the source whence my being was derived, but he is the fountain whence I derive all my good; in whom, says David, I will trust. And why? Because he knew him to be an eternal and inexhaustible fountain of goodness. This fine idea is lost in our translation; for we render two Hebrew words of widely different meaning, by the same term in English, strength. <div eID="gen18984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18985" type="x-p"/> 7. My buckler, מגני maginni, my shield, my defender, he who covers my head and my heart, so that I am neither slain nor wounded by the darts of my adversaries. <div eID="gen18985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18986" type="x-p"/> 8. Horn of my salvation. Horn was the emblem of power, and power in exercise. This has been already explained; see on <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.1">1Sam 2:1</reference> (note). The horn of salvation means a powerful, an efficient salvation. <div eID="gen18986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18987" type="x-p"/> 9. My high tourer; not only a place of defense, but one from which I can discern the country round about, and always be able to discover danger before it approaches me.
entries.d70467e00b3700b90a48a4c185b6a6a655df7c86: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen18987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18988" type="x-p"/> I will call upon the Lord - When he was conscious that the object of his worship was such as he has pointed out in the above nine particulars, it is no wonder that he resolves to call upon him; and no wonder that he expects, in consequence, to be saved from his enemies; for who can destroy him whom such a God undertakes to save?
entries.d0c379095c5eeb1cded239af73e4a0f0a278064f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen18988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18989" type="x-p"/> The sorrows of death compassed me - חבלי מות chebley maveth, the cables or cords of death. He was almost taken in those nets or stratagems by which, if he had been entangled, he would have lost his life. The stratagems to which he refers were those that were intended for his destruction; hence called the cables or cords of death. <div eID="gen18989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18990" type="x-p"/> The floods of ungodly men - Troops of wicked men were rushing upon him like an irresistible torrent; or like the waves of the sea, one impelling another forward in successive ranks; so that, thinking he must be overwhelmed by them, he was for the moment affrighted; but God turned the torrent aside, and he escaped.
entries.7e22f991b3209e2c1ab08dafa8565a79f6aba786: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen18990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18991" type="x-p"/> The sorrows of hell - חבלי שאול chebley sheol, the cables or cords of the grave. Is not this a reference to the cords or ropes with which they lowered the corpse into the grave? or the bandages by which the dead were swathed? He was as good as dead. <div eID="gen18991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18992" type="x-p"/> The snares of death prevented me - I was just on the point of dropping into the pit which they had digged for me. In short, I was all but a dead man; and nothing less than the immediate interference of God could have saved my life.
entries.6f882a1754c301414e9568825d16b0e92eedd813: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen18992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18993" type="x-p"/> In my distress I called - His enemies had no hope of his destruction unless God should abandon him. They hoped that this was the case, and that therefore they should prevail. But God heard his cry and came down to his help; and this interference is most majestically described in the <reference osisRef="Psa.18.7">Psa 18:7</reference> and following verses. Dr. Dodd has collected some excellent observations on these verses from Chandler, Delaney, and others, which I shall transcribe, as I know not that any thing better can be offered on the subject.
entries.580cae928924671739c146e7366e741400df1433: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen18993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18994" type="x-p"/> Then the earth shook and trembled - "In this and the following verses David describes, by the sublimest expressions and grandest terms, the majesty of God, and the awful manner in which he came to his assistance. The representation of the storm in these verses must be allowed by all skillful and impartial judges to be truly sublime and noble, and in the genuine spirit of poetry. The majesty of God, and the manner in which he is represented as coming to the aid of his favourite king, surrounded with all the powers of nature as his attendants and ministers, and arming (as it were) heaven and earth to fight his battles, and execute his vengeance, is described in the loftiest and most striking terms. The shaking of the earth; the trembling of the mountains and pillars of heaven; the smoke that drove out of his nostrils; the flames of devouring fire that flashed from his mouth; the heavens bending down to convey him to the battle; his riding upon a cherub, and rapidly flying on the wings of a whirlwind; his concealing his majesty in the thick clouds of heaven; the bursting of the lightnings from the horrid darkness; the uttering of his voice in peals of thunder; the storm of fiery hail; the melting of the heavens, and their dissolving into floods of tempestuous rain; the cleaving of the earth, and disclosing of the bottom of the hills, and the subterraneous channels or torrents of water, by the very breath of the nostrils of the Almighty; are all of them circumstances which create admiration, excite a kind of horror, and exceed every thing of this nature that is to be found in any of the remains of heathen antiquity. See Longinus on the Sublime, sec. 9, and Hesiod's description of Jupiter fighting against the Titans, which is one of the grandest things in all pagan antiquity; though upon comparison it will be found infinitely short of this description of the psalmist's; throughout the whole of which God is represented as a mighty warrior going forth to fight the battles of David, and highly incensed at the opposition his enemies made to his power and authority. "When he descended to the engagement the very heavens bowed down to render his descent more awful, his military tent was substantial darkness; the voice of his thunder was the warlike alarm which sounded to the battle; the chariot in which he rode was the thick clouds of heaven, conducted by cherubs, and carried on by the irresistible force and rapid wings of an impetuous tempest; and the darts and weapons he employed were thunderbolts, lightnings, fiery hail, deluging rains, and stormy winds! "No wonder that when God thus arose, all his enemies should be scattered, and those who hated him should flee before him. "It does not appear from any part of David's history that there was any such storm as is here described, which proved destructive to his enemies, and salutary to himself. There might, indeed, have been such a one, though there is no particular mention of it: unless it may be thought that something of this nature is intimated in the account given of David's second battle with the Philistines, <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.23">2Sam 5:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.24">2Sam 5:24</reference>. It is undoubted, however, that the storm is represented as real; though David, in describing it, has heightened and embellished it with all the ornaments of poetry. See Chandler, Delaney, and Lowth's ninth Prelection.
entries.1a8a5aaf0662a34b847604d7b150ae7d5e47d8d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen18994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18995" type="x-p"/> There went up a smoke out of his nostrils - Or, 'There ascended into his nostrils a smoke,' as the words, literally rendered, signify. The ancients placed the seat of anger in the nose, or nostrils; because when the passions are warm and violent, it discovers itself by the heated vehement breath which proceeds from them. Hence the physiognomists considered open wide nostrils as a sign of an angry, fiery disposition. "This description of a smoke arising into and a fire breaking forth from the nostrils of God, denotes, by a poetical figure, the greatness of his anger and indignation. "Fire out of his mouth devoured - means that consuming fire issued out of his mouth. Coals were kind led by it, thus we render the next clause; but the words do not mean that fire proceeding from God kindled coals, but that burning coals issued from his mouth; and it should be rendered 'living coals from his mouth burned, and consumed around him.' - Chandler.
entries.a23fe03b0bbb8577412712839aa1ad31e12a1032: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen18995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18996" type="x-p"/> He bowed the heavens also, and came down - He made the heavens bend under him when he descended to take vengeance on his enemies. The psalmist seems here to express the appearance of the Divine majesty in a glorious cloud, descending from heaven, which underneath was substantially dark, but above, bright, and shining with exceeding lustre; and which, by its gradual approach to the earth, would appear as though the heavens themselves were bending down and approaching towards us.
entries.71f213217debb0ac399c62cb675cfcbac6e941f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen18996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18997" type="x-p"/> He rode upon a cherub, and did fly - That is, as it is immediately explained, Yea, he did fly upon the wings of the wind. God was in the storm, and by the ministry of angels guided the course of it, and drove it on with such an impetuous force as nothing could withstand. He 'rides in the whirlwind and directs the storm.' Angels are in a peculiar sense the attendants and messengers of the Almighty, whom he employs as his ministers in effecting many of those great events which take place in the administration of his providence; and particularly such as manifest his immediate interposition in the extraordinary judgments which he inflicts for the punishment of sinful nations. See <reference osisRef="Psa.103.20">Psa 103:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.104.4">Psa 104:4</reference>. The cherub is particularly mentioned as an emblem of the Divine presence, and especially as employed in supporting and conveying the chariot of the Almighty, when he is represented as riding in his majesty through the firmament of heaven: - - Forth rush'd with whirlwind sound <div eID="gen18997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18998" type="x-p"/> The chariot of paternal Deity; <div eID="gen18998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18999" type="x-p"/> Flashing thick flames, wheel within wheel undrawn, <div eID="gen18999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19000" type="x-p"/> Itself instinct with spirit, but convey'd <div eID="gen19000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19001" type="x-p"/> By four cherubic shapes. <div eID="gen19001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19002" type="x-p"/> Par. Lost, lib. vi. <div eID="gen19002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19003" type="x-p"/> This seems to be the image intended to be conveyed in the place before us. "He rode upon a cherub, and did fly; he flew on the wings of the wind," i.e., the cherub supported and led on the tempest, in which the Almighty rode as in his chariot. This is agreeable to the office elsewhere ascribed to the cherubim. Thus they supported the mercy-seat, which was peculiarly the throne of God under the Jewish economy. God is expressly said to "make the clouds his chariot," <reference osisRef="Psa.104.3">Psa 104:3</reference>; and to "ride upon a swift cloud," <reference osisRef="Isa.19.1">Isa 19:1</reference> : so that "riding upon a cherub," and "riding upon a swift cloud," is riding in the cloud as his chariot, supported and guided by the ministry of the cherubim. The next clause in the parallel place of Samuel is, "He was seen on the wings of the wind;" ירא yera, he was seen, being used for ידא yede, he flew, ד daleth being changed into ר resh. Either of them may be the true reading, for the MSS. are greatly divided on these places; but on the whole וירא vaiyera appears to be the better reading: "And he was seen on the wings of the wind." <div eID="gen19003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19004" type="x-p"/> As the original has been supposed by adequate judges to exhibit a fine specimen of that poetry which, in the choice of its terms, conveys both sense and sound, I will again lay it before the reader, as I have done in the parallel place, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.2">2Sam 22:2</reference>. The words in italic to be read from right to left. ויעף כרוב על וירכב vaiyaoph kerub al vayirkab And he rode upon a cherub, and did fly! רוח כנפי על וידא ruach canphey al waiyede Yea, he flew on the wings of the wind! The word רוח ruach, in the last line, should be pronounced, not ruak, which is no Hebrew word: but as a Scottish man would pronounce it, were it written ruagh. With this observation, how astonishingly is the rushing of the wind heard in the last word of each hemistich! Sternhold and Hopkins have succeeded in their version of this place, not only beyond all they ever did, but beyond every ancient and modern poet on a similar subject: - "On cherub and on cherubinFull royally he rode; <div eID="gen19004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19005" type="x-p"/> And on the wings of mighty windsCame flying all abroad." <div eID="gen19005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19006" type="x-p"/> Even the old Anglo-Scottish Psalter has not done amiss: - <div eID="gen19006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19007" type="x-p"/> And he steygh aboven cherubyn and he flow; <div eID="gen19007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19008" type="x-p"/> He flow aboven the fethers of wyndes.
entries.f86f6cc1878471b595323a1352d16916a78a9cd4: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen19008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19009" type="x-p"/> He made darkness his secret place - God is represented as dwelling in the thick darkness, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.11">Deu 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.97.2">Psa 97:2</reference>. This representation in the place before us is peculiarly proper; as thick heavy clouds deeply charged, and with lowering aspects, are always the forerunners and attendants of a tempest, and greatly heighten the horrors of the appearance: and the representation of them, spread about the Almighty as a tent, is truly grand and poetic. <div eID="gen19009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19010" type="x-p"/> Dark waters - The vapors strongly condensed into clouds; which, by the stroke of the lightning, are about to be precipitated in torrents of rain. See the next verse.
entries.a49a66e056062927eab72cf4eaff3966ec8575c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen19010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19011" type="x-p"/> At the brightness that was before him his thick clouds passed - The word נגה nogah signifies the lightning. This goes before him: the flash is seen before the thunder is heard, and before the rain descends; and then the thick cloud passes. Its contents are precipitated on the earth, and the cloud is entirely dissipated. <div eID="gen19011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19012" type="x-p"/> Hail-stones and coals of fire - This was the storm that followed the flash and the peal; for it is immediately added: -
entries.19281c40441c3fe5e2c5353b14187090a04e7b8d: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen19012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19013" type="x-p"/> The Lord also thundered in the heavens, and the Highest gave his voice - And then followed the hail and coals of fire. The former verse mentioned the lightning, with its effects; this gives us the report of the thunder, and the increasing storm of hail and fire that attended it. Some think the words hail-stones and coals of fire are entered here by some careless transcribers from the preceding verse; and it is true that they are wanting in the Septuagint and the Arabic, in the parallel place in 2 Samuel, and in five of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. I should rather, with Bishop Horsley, suppose them to be an interpolation in the preceding verse: or in that to have been borrowed from this; for this most certainly is their true place.
entries.f973667eba65f494a56b8828c63df7a525b425b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen19013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19014" type="x-p"/> Be sent out his arrows - he shot out lightning - I believe the latter clause to be an illustration of the former. He sent out his arrows - that is, he shot out lightning; for lightnings are the arrows of the Lord, and there is something very like the arrowhead apparent in the zigzag lightning. Sense and sound are wonderfully combined in the Hebrew of this last clause: וברכים רב ויהמם uberakim rab vaihummem, "and thunderings he multiplied and confounded them." Who does not hear the bursting, brattling, and pounding of thunder in these words? See Delaney?
entries.f266798cf0274f12a0031fdabf695c223b8c62b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen19014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19015" type="x-p"/> The channels of water were seen - This must refer to an earthquake; for in such cases, the ground being rent, water frequently gushes out at the fissures, and often rises to a tremendous height. Whole rivers were poured out of the chasms made by the earthquake in Jamaica, A. D. 1694; and new lakes of water were formed, covering a thousand acres of land!
entries.f033e442fbb764e1fce65470c2589b5b66174c22: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen19015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19016" type="x-p"/> He drew me out of many waters - Here the allusion is still carried on. The waters thus poured out were sweeping the people away; but God, by a miraculous interference, sent and drew David out. Sometimes waters are used to denote multitudes of people; and here the word may have that reference; multitudes were gathered together against David, but God delivered him from them all. This seems to be countenanced by the following verse.
entries.e1d857a94e4659e37b1bd4ddca60ccb5a8292ab8: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen19016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19017" type="x-p"/> He delivered me from my strong enemy - Does not this refer to his conflict with Ishbi-benob? "And Ishbi-benob, which was of the sons of the giant - thought to have slain David. But Abishai the son of Zeruiah succoured him, and smote the Philistine, and killed him. Then the men of David sware unto him, saying, Thou shalt go no more out with us to battle, that thou quench not the light of Israel;" <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.16">2Sam 21:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.17">2Sam 21:17</reference>. It appears that at this time he was in the most imminent danger of his life, and that he must have fallen by the hands of the giant, if God had not sent Abishai to his assistance. They were too strong for me. He was nearly overpowered by the Philistines; and his escape was such as evidently to show it to be supernatural.
entries.44552c0396e27f91af4dacda2af3e8fad3a67661: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen19017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19018" type="x-p"/> They prevented me in the day of my calamity - They took advantage of the time in which I was least able to make head against them, and their attack was sudden and powerful. I should have been overthrown, but the Lord was my stay. He had been nearly exhausted by the fatigue of the day, when the giant availed himself of this advantage.
entries.866541a8b16784dfafbb4780a22ace3843148c51: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen19018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19019" type="x-p"/> He brought me forth also into a large place - He enabled me to clear the country of my foes, who had before cooped me up in holes and corners. This appears to be the allusion.
entries.f1c91471dd00769ae5f93c42ae5a0166f6c9ab90: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen19019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19020" type="x-p"/> The Lord rewarded me - David proceeds to give the reasons why God had so marvellously interposed in his behalf. <div eID="gen19020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19021" type="x-p"/> According to my righteousness - Instead of being an enemy to Saul, I was his friend. I dealt righteously with him while he dealt unrighteously with me.
entries.3cf0163db256d6ec96e6577481bd25471ec0898f: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen19021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19022" type="x-p"/> I have kept the ways of the Lord - I was neither an infidel nor a profligate; I trusted in God, and carefully observed all the ordinances of his religion.
entries.97b5210d050bc59467dad32c2c563399cebec0a6: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen19022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19023" type="x-p"/> All his judgments were before me - I kept his law before my eyes, that I might see my duty and know how to walk and please God.
entries.84897a17a7cd07c82e2a95236871596291184c70: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen19023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19024" type="x-p"/> I was also upright - The times in which David was most afflicted were the times of his greatest uprightness. Adversity was always to him a time of spiritual prosperity. <div eID="gen19024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19025" type="x-p"/> Mine iniquity - Probably meaning what is generally termed the easily-besetting sin; the sin of his constitution, or that to which the temperament of his body most powerfully disposed him. What this was, is a subject of useless conjecture.
entries.1b799714a891da23aff642e05bf91195d01ffea5: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen19025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19026" type="x-p"/> With the merciful thou wilt show thyself merciful - Thou wilt deal with men as they deal with each other. This is the general tenor of God's providential conduct towards mankind; well expressed by Mr. Pope in his universal prayer: - "Teach me to feel another's wo;To hide the fault I see: <div eID="gen19026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19027" type="x-p"/> The mercy I to others show,That mercy show to me." <div eID="gen19027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19028" type="x-p"/> It is in reference to this that our Lord teaches us to pray: "Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive them that trespass against us." If we act feelingly and mercifully towards our fellow creatures, God will act tenderly and compassionately towards us. The merciful, the upright, and the pure, will ever have the God of mercy, uprightness, and purity, to defend and support them.
entries.2cb123a8e90147a7bb83d5c30fe42cdff3cc8c2a: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen19028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19029" type="x-p"/> With the froward - עקש ikkesh, the perverse man; he that is crooked in his tempers and ways. <div eID="gen19029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19030" type="x-p"/> Thou wilt show thyself froward - תתפתל tithpattal, thou wilt set thyself to twist, twine, and wrestle. If he contend, thou wilt contend with him. Thou wilt follow him through all his windings; thou wilt trace him through all his crooked ways; untwist him in all his cunning wiles; and defeat all his schemes of stubbornness, fraud, overreaching, and deceit. <div eID="gen19030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19031" type="x-p"/> My old Psalter has, With the wiked thow sal be wike. Here the term wicked is taken in its true original sense, crooked, or perverse. With the wiked, the perverse, thou wilt show thyself wike, i.e., perverse; from to draw back, to slide. As he draws back from thee, thou wilt draw back from him. It may, as before intimated, come from to seek for enchantments; leaving God, and going to devils; to act like a witch: but here it must mean as above. The plain import is, "If thou perversely oppose thy Maker, he will oppose thee: no work or project shall prosper that is not begun in his name, and conducted in his fear."
entries.e3297aa30ca8e41e8c700aa6312c5a1db7456266: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen19031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19032" type="x-p"/> For thou wilt save the afflicted - The afflicted are the humble; and those thou hast ever befriended.
entries.defabf8807256575faf7f19b71dcf14b8e944d5b: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen19032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19033" type="x-p"/> For thou wilt light my candle - Thou wilt restore me to prosperity, and give me a happy issue out of all my afflictions. By the lamp of David the Messiah may be meant: thou wilt not suffer my family to become extinct, nor the kingdom which thou hast promised me utterly to fail.
entries.76561b19b02b728ffaca6ef510003448946d4293: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen19033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19034" type="x-p"/> I have run through a troop - This may relate to some remarkable victory, and the taking of some fortified place, possibly Zion, from the Jebusites. See the account <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.6-2Sam.5.8">2Sam 5:6-8</reference> (note).
entries.93e841e7b6e943481eed8954b426896baa9dac07: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen19034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19035" type="x-p"/> God, his way is perfect - His conduct is like his nature, absolutely pure. <div eID="gen19035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19036" type="x-p"/> The word of the Lord is tried - Literally tried in the fire. It has stood all tests; and has never failed those who pleaded it before its author. <div eID="gen19036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19037" type="x-p"/> He is a buckler - A sure protection to every simple believing soul. We cannot believe his word too implicity; nor trust too confidently in him.
entries.c263c8b380ed6af93212c3aaa1b5b94f2a079914: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen19037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19038" type="x-p"/> For who is God save the Lord? - "For who is Eloah, except Jehovah?" None is worthy of adoration but the self-existent, eternal, infinitely perfect, and all-merciful Being. <div eID="gen19038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19039" type="x-p"/> Or who is a rock - A fountain emitting continual supplies of grace and goodness.
