entries.8ea5cd1d32f248aa19d942bab225e87792b759ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen19039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19040" type="x-p"/> God - girdeth me with strength - The girdle was a necessary part of the Eastern dress; it strengthened and supported the loins; served to confine the garments close to the body; and in it they tucked them up when journeying. The strength of God was to his soul what the girdle was to the body. I need not add, that the girdle was also an ornamental part of the dress, and from it the sword was suspended. <div eID="gen19040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19041" type="x-p"/> And maketh my way perfect - He directs me so that I do not go astray; he blesses me in my undertakings; and by him the issue of my labors is crowned with prosperity.
entries.920709060739aadad33d4e6f3ab977712b901058: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen19041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19042" type="x-p"/> My feet like hinds' feet - Swiftness, or speed of foot, was a necessary qualification of an ancient hero. This was of great advantage in pursuing, combating, or escaping from a fallen foe. Ποδας ωκυς Αχιλλευς, "the swiftfooted Achilles," is frequently given by Homer as a most honorable qualification of his hero. <div eID="gen19042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19043" type="x-p"/> Upon my high places - In allusion to the hinds, antelopes, mountain goats, etc., which frequented such places, and in which they found both food and safety. God frequently preserved the life of David by means of these.
entries.577a8ab2e24f90df7420b01f4a3c92bbd2b148d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen19043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19044" type="x-p"/> He teacheth my hands to war - The success which I have had in my military exercises I owe to the Divine help. How few of the conquerors of mankind can say so! And how few among those who call themselves Christian warriors dare to say so! War is as contrary to the spirit of Christianity as murder. Nothing can justify Christian nations in shedding each other's blood! All men should live in peace; all men might live in peace; and the nation that is first to break it is under a heavy curse. <div eID="gen19044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19045" type="x-p"/> A bow of steel is broken by mine arms - All the versions render this: "Thou hast made my arm like a brazen bow." A bow of steel is out of the question. In the days of David it is not likely that the method of making steel was known. The method of making brass out of copper was known at a very early period of the world; and the ancients had the art of hardening it, so as to work it into the most efficient swords. From his own account David was swift, courageous, and strong.
entries.0f0d88777141eacf22e72715d5e1702803992494: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen19045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19046" type="x-p"/> The shield of thy salvation - In all battles and dangers God defended him. He was constantly safe because he possessed the salvation of God. Everywhere God protected him. Thy gentleness, ענותך anvathecha, thy meekness or humility. Thou hast enabled me to bear and forbear; to behave with courage in adversity, and with humility in prosperity; and thus I am become great. By these means thou hast multiplied me. The Vulgate reads, Disciplina tua ipsa me docebit; "And thy discipline itself shall teach me." In this sense it was understood by most of the versions. The old Psalter paraphrases thus: Thi chastying suffers me noght to erre fra the end to com.
entries.2ca47ebcd31843d7e7f671b1ffbae43283a7d030: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen19046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19047" type="x-p"/> Enlarged my steps - See on <reference osisRef="Psa.18.19">Psa 18:19</reference> (note). From the hand of God he had continual prosperity; and while he walked with God no enemy was able to prevail against him. He details his successes in the following verses.
entries.e5be3417c4d107b8af7bb0e2858b6d0376d2c09d: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen19047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19048" type="x-p"/> The necks of mine enemies - Thou hast made me a complete conqueror. Treading on the neck of an enemy was the triumph of the conqueror, and the utmost disgrace of the vanquished.
entries.6c6da19085f3b581497bbd0cf9281b2a05171b17: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen19048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19049" type="x-p"/> They cited - The Philistines called upon their gods, but there was none to save them. <div eID="gen19049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19050" type="x-p"/> Even unto the Lord - Such as Saul, Ishbosheth, Absalom, etc., who, professing to worship the true God, called on him while in their opposition to David; but God no more heard them than their idols heard the Philistines.
entries.e9acc0d4e06910e9970f50a8e336b8ef0cbdc862: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen19050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19051" type="x-p"/> Then did I beat them - God was with him, and they had only an arm of flesh. No wonder then that his enemies were destroyed. <div eID="gen19051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19052" type="x-p"/> Small as the dust before the wind - This well expresses the manner in which he treated the Moabites, Ammonites, and the people of Rabbah: "He put them under saws, and under harrows of iron, and under axes of iron; and made them pass through the brick-kiln," etc. See <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.31">2Sam 12:31</reference> (note), and the notes there.
entries.0a8451e532742d71e4e643c325c0b09c5cf00267: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen19052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19053" type="x-p"/> The strivings of the people - Disaffections and insurrections among my own subjects, as in the revolt of Absalom, the civil war of Abner in favor of Ish-bosheth, etc. <div eID="gen19053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19054" type="x-p"/> The head of the heathen - ראש גוים rosh goyim, "the chief," or "governor, of the nations;" all the circumjacent heathen people; all these were subdued by David, and brought under tribute. <div eID="gen19054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19055" type="x-p"/> A people whom I have not known - The people whom he knew were those of the twelve tribes; those whom he did not know were the Syrians, Philistines, Idumeans, etc. All these served him, that is, paid him tribute.
entries.69648aa1c8be7c6fb91f57a5e13edd88b40cbf3c: <hi type="bold">Verse 44</hi> <div eID="gen19055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19056" type="x-p"/> As soon as they hear of me - His victories were so rapid and splendid over powerful enemies, that they struck a general terror among the people, and several submitted without a contest. <div eID="gen19056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19057" type="x-p"/> Strangers shall submit themselves unto me - Some translate this: "The children of the foreign woman have lied unto me." This has been understood two ways: My own people, who have sworn fealty to me, have broken their obligation, and followed my rebellious son. Or, The heathens, who have been brought under my yoke, have promised the most cordial obedience, and flattered me with their tongues, while their hearts felt enmity against me and my government. Nevertheless, even in this unwilling subjection I was secure, my police being so efficient, and my kingdom so strong.
entries.1532575cc5e1f868a7ce5ce3f016472645d2dc0f: <hi type="bold">Verse 45</hi> <div eID="gen19057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19058" type="x-p"/> The strangers shall fade away - בני נכר beney nechar, the same persons mentioned above. They shall not be able to effect any thing against me; יבלו yibbolu, "they shall fall as the leaves fall off the trees in winter." <div eID="gen19058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19059" type="x-p"/> And be afraid out of their close places - Those who have formed themselves into banditti, and have taken possession of rocks and fortified places, shall be so afraid when they hear of my successes, that they shall surrender at discretion, without standing a siege. Perhaps all these verbs should be understood in the perfect tense, for David is here evidently speaking of a kingdom at rest, all enemies having been subdued; or, as the title is, when the Lord Had delivered him from all his enemies.
entries.83c09056dc5f8d63740e9e04d2a1eff478946962: <hi type="bold">Verse 46</hi> <div eID="gen19059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19060" type="x-p"/> The Lord liveth - By him alone I have gained all my victories; and he continueth, and will be my Rock, the Source whence I may at all times derive help and salvation. May his name be blessed! May his kingdom be exalted!
entries.1eb3bd2cbe45f8bb78e536e5301d1e65382b78c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 47</hi> <div eID="gen19060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19061" type="x-p"/> God that avengeth me - The way that I took was after his own heart; therefore he sustained me in it, and did me justice over my enemies. <div eID="gen19061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19062" type="x-p"/> Subdueth the people under me - He keeps down the spirits of the disaffected, and weakens their hands. They are subdued, and they continue under me; and this is the Lord's doing.
entries.248e1601c6f34a2385652d2c47ec6629288d3faf: <hi type="bold">Verse 48</hi> <div eID="gen19062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19063" type="x-p"/> He delivereth me - That is, he hath delivered me, and continues to deliver me, from all that rise up against me. <div eID="gen19063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19064" type="x-p"/> The violent man - Saul; this applies particularly to him.
entries.b43872e439101d6ae4a469f12a53f3c2e1941be1: <hi type="bold">Verse 49</hi> <div eID="gen19064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19065" type="x-p"/> WilI I give thanks unto thee - among the heathen - Quoted by St. Paul, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.9">Rom 15:9</reference>, to prove that the calling of the Gentiles was predicted, and that what then took place was the fulfillment of that prediction. <div eID="gen19065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19066" type="x-p"/> But there is a sense in which it applies particularly to David, well observed by Theodoret: "We see," says he, "evidently the fulfillment of this prophecy; for even to the present day David praises the Lord among the Gentiles by the mouth of true believers; seeing there is not a town, village, hamlet, country, nor even a desert, where Christians dwell, in which God is not praised by their singing the Psalms of David."
entries.8ef77e84365022783813a6450ebccacedce627c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 50</hi> <div eID="gen19066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19067" type="x-p"/> Great deliverance giveth he to his king - David was a king of God's appointment, and was peculiarly favored by him. Literally, He is magnifying the salvations of his king. He not only delivers, but follows up those deliverances with innumerable blessings. <div eID="gen19067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19068" type="x-p"/> Showeth mercy - to David - I have no claim upon his bounty. I deserve nothing from him, but he continues to show mercy. <div eID="gen19068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19069" type="x-p"/> To his seed - His posterity. So the words זרע zera and σπερμα, in the Old and New Testament, should be universally translated. The common translation is totally improper, and now more so than formerly, when anatomy was less understood. <div eID="gen19069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19070" type="x-p"/> For evermore - עד עולם ad olam, for ever; through all duration of created worlds. And more - the eternity that is beyond time. This shows that another David is meant, with another kind of posterity, and another sort of kingdom. From the family of David came the man Christ Jesus; his posterity are the genuine Christians; his kingdom, in which they are subjects, is spiritual. This government shall last through all time, for Christianity will continue to prevail till the end of the world: and it will be extended through eternity; for that is the kingdom of glory in which Jesus reigns on the throne of his Father, and in which his followers shall reign with him for ever and ever. <div eID="gen19070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19071" type="x-p"/> It has already been remarked that this whole Psalm has been understood as relating to the passion and victories of Christ, and the success of the Gospel in the earth. In this way Bishop Horne has understood and paraphrased it; and in the same way it is considered by the ancient Psalter, so often mentioned. Many of the primitive fathers and modern interpreters have taken the same view of it. Those passages which I judged to have this meaning I have pointed out, and have only to add that, as David was a type of Christ, many things spoken of him primarily, refer to our Lord ultimately; but much judgment and caution are required in their application. To apply the whole Psalm in this way appears to me very injudicious, and often derogatory from the majesty of Christ. Let this be my excuse for not following the same track in which many of my predecessors have gone.  <chapter eID="Ps.18"/> <div eID="gen19071" type="x-p"/>

entries.3b837462858169fac3bd84479aaab0d4b5016c4a: <div eID="gen9202" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">David’s Hymnic Retrospect of a Life Crowned with Many Mercies</title> <div sID="gen9203" type="x-p"/> Next to a תּפּלּה of David comes a שׁירה (<hi type="italic">nom. unitatis</hi> from שׁיר), which is in many ways both in words and thoughts (<hi type="italic">Symbolae</hi> p. 49) interwoven with the former. It is the longest of all the hymnic Psalms, and bears the inscription: <hi type="italic">To the Precentor, by the servant of Jahve, by David, who spake unto Jahve the words of this song in the day that Jahve had delivered him out of the hand of all his enemies and out of the hand of Saûl : then he said. </hi> The original inscription of the Psalm in the primary collection was probably only לדוד למנצח לעבד ה, like the inscription of <reference osisRef="Ps.36.1">Psa 36:1</reference>-12. The rest of the inscription resembles the language with which songs of this class are wont to be introduced in their connection in the historical narrative, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.1">Exo 15:1</reference>; Num 21:17, and more especially Deu 31:30. And the Psalm before us is found again in 2 Sam 22, introduced by words, the manifestly unaccidental agreement of which with the inscription in the Psalter, is explained by its having been incorporated in one of the histories from which the Books of Samuel are extracted, - probably the Annals (<hi type="italic">Dibre ha-Jamim</hi>) of David. From this source the writer of the Books of Samuel has taken the Psalm, together with that introduction; and from this source also springs the historical portion of the inscription in the Psalter, which is connected with the preceding by אשׁר. <div eID="gen9203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9204" type="x-p"/> David may have styled himself in the inscription עבד ה, just as the apostles call themselves δοῦλοι Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. He also in other instances, in prayer, calls himself “the servant of Jahve,” <reference osisRef="Ps.19.12">Psa 19:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.14">Psa 19:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.144.10">Psa 144:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.20">2Sa 7:20</reference>, as every Israelite might do; but David, who is the first after Moses and Joshua to bear this designation or by-name, could to so in an especial sense. For he, with whom the kingship of promise began, marks an epoch in his service of the work of God no less than did Moses, through whose mediation Israel received the Law, and Joshua, through whose instrumentality they obtained the Land of promise. <div eID="gen9204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9205" type="x-p"/> The terminology of psalm-poesy does not include the word שׁירה, but only שׁיר. This at once shows that the historical portion of the inscription comes from some other source. בּיום is followed, not by the <hi type="italic">infin</hi>. הצּיל: on the day of deliverance, but by the more exactly <hi type="italic">plusquamperf</hi>. הצּיל: on the day (בּיום = at the time, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.2.4">Gen 2:4</reference>, and frequently) when he had delivered - a genitival (Ges. §116, 3) relative clause, like <reference osisRef="Ps.138.3">Psa 138:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.6.28">Exo 6:28</reference>; Num 3:1, cf. Psa 56:10. מיּד alternates with מכּף in this text without any other design than that of varying the expression. The deliverance out of the hand of Saul is made specially prominent, because the most prominent portion of the Psalm, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.5">Psa 18:5</reference>, treats of it. The danger in which David the was placed, was of the most personal, the most perilous, and the most protracted kind. This prominence was of great service to the collector, because the preceding Psalm bears the features of this time, the lamentations over which are heard there and further back, and now all find expression in this more extended song of praise. <div eID="gen9205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9206" type="x-p"/> Only a fondness for doubt can lead any one to doubt the Davidic origin of this Psalm, attested as it is in two works, which are independent of one another. The twofold testimony of tradition is supported by the fact that the Psalm contains nothing that militates against David being the author; even the mention of his own name at the close, is not against it (cf. 1Ki 2:45). We have before us an Israelitish counterpart to the cuneiform monumental inscriptions, in which the kings of worldly monarchies recapitulate the deeds they have done by the help of their gods. The speaker is a king; the author of the Books of Samuel found the song already in existence as a Davidic song; the difference of his text from that which lies before us in the Psalter, shows that at that time it had been transmitted from some earlier period; writers of the later time of the kings here and there use language which is borrowed from it or are echoes of it (comp. <reference osisRef="Prov.30.5">Pro 30:5</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.18.31">Psa 18:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.19">Hab 3:19</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.18.34">Psa 18:34</reference>); it bears throughout the mark of the classic age of the language and poetry, and “if it be not David’s, it must have been written in his name and by some one imbued with his spirit, and who could have been this contemporary poet and twin-genius?” (Hitzig). All this irresistibly points us to David himself, to whom really belong also all the other songs in the Second Book of Samuel, which are introduced as Davidic (over Saul and Jonathan, over Abner, etc.). This, the greatest of all, springs entirely from the new self-consciousness to which he was raised by the promises recorded in 2 Sam 7; ; and towards the end, it closes with express retrospective reference to these promises; for David’s certainty of the everlasting duration of his house, and God’s covenant of mercy with his house, rests upon the announcement made by Nathan. <div eID="gen9206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9207" type="x-p"/> The Psalm divides into two halves; for the strain of praise begins anew with <reference osisRef="Ps.18.32">Psa 18:32</reference>, after having run its first course and come to a beautiful close in Psa 18:31. The two halves are also distinct in respect of their artificial form. The strophe schema of the first is: 6. 8. 8. 6. 8 (not 9). 8. 8. 8. 7. The mixture of six and eight line strophes is symmetrical, and the seven of the last strophe is nothing strange. The mixture in the second half on the contrary is varied. The art of the strophe system appears here, as is also seen in other instances in the Psalms, to be relaxed; and the striving after form at the commencement has given way to the pressure and crowding of the thoughts. <div eID="gen9207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9208" type="x-p"/> The traditional mode of writing out this Psalm, as also the <hi type="italic">Cantica</hi>, 2 Sam 22 and Judg 5, is “a half-brick upon a brick, and a brick upon a half-brick” (אירח על גבי לבנה ולבנה על גבי אריח): i.e., one line consisting of two, and one of three parts of a verse, and the line consisting of the three parts has only one word on the right and on the left; the whole consequently forms three columns. On the other hand, the song in Deut 32 (as also Jos 12:9., <reference osisRef="Esth.9.7-Esth.9.10">Est 9:7-10</reference>) is to be written “a half-brick upon a half-brick and a brick upon a brick,” i.e., in only two columns, cf. <hi type="italic">infra</hi> p. 269.
entries.ddee0d38bc1c85e2ffbaadecff9fdfdd56c82e82: <reference osisRef="Ps.18.1-Ps.18.3">Psa 18:1-3</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_18:2-4) The poet opens with a number of endearing names for God, in which he gratefully comprehends the results of long and varied experience. So far as regards the parallelism of the members, a monostich forms the beginning of this Psalm, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1-Ps.16.11">Psa 16:1-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.23.1-Ps.23.6">Psa 23:1-6</reference>; Ps 25 and many others. Nevertheless the matter assumes a somewhat different aspect, if <reference osisRef="Ps.18.3">Psa 18:3</reference> is not, with Maurer, Hengstenberg and Hupfeld, taken as two predicate clauses (Jahve is..., my God is...), but as a simple vocative-a rendering which alone corresponds to the intensity with which this greatest of the Davidic hymns opens-God being invoked by ה, ה, אלי, and each of these names being followed by a predicative expansion of itself, which increases in fulness of tone and emphasis. The ארחמך (with <hi type="italic">ā</hi>, according to Ew. §251, <hi type="italic">b</hi>), which carries the three series of the names of God, makes up in depth of meaning what is wanting in compass. Elsewhere we find only the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> רחם of tender sympathising love, but here the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> is used as an Aramaism. Hence the Jalkut on this passages explains it by רחמאי יתך “I love thee,” or ardent, heartfelt love and attachment. The primary signification of softness (root רח, Arab.<hi type="italic">rḥ , rch</hi>, to be soft, lax, loose), whence רחם, <hi type="italic">uterus</hi>, is transferred in both cases to tenderness of feeling or sentiment. The most general predicate חזפי (from חזק according to a similar inflexion to אמר, בּסר, עמק, <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. עמקי <reference osisRef="Prov.9.18">Pro 9:18</reference>) is followed by those which describe Jahve as a protector and deliverer in persecution on the one hand, and on the other as a defender and the giver of victory in battle. They are all typical names symbolising what Jahve is in Himself; hence instead of וּמפלּטי it would perhaps have been more correct to point וּמפלטי (and my refuge). God had already called Himself a shield to Abram, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.1">Gen 15:1</reference>; and He is called צוּר (cf. אבן <reference osisRef="Gen.49.24">Gen 49:24</reference>) in the great Mosaic song, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.4">Deu 32:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.37">Deu 32:37</reference> (the latter verse is distinctly echoed here). סלע from סלע, Arab. <hi type="italic">sl‛ , findere</hi>, means properly a cleft in a rock (Arabic סלע,<note placement="foot">Neshwân defines thus: Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - sal‛</hi> is a cutting in a mountain after the manner of a gorge; and Jâkût, who cites a number of places that are so called: a wide plain (Arab. <hi type="italic">fḍ'</hi>) enclosed by steep rocks, which is reached through a narrow pass (Arab. <hi type="italic">ša‛b</hi>), but can only be descended on foot. Accordingly, in סלעי the idea of a safe (and comfortable) hiding-place preponderates; in צוּרי that of firm ground and inaccessibility. The one figure calls to mind the (well-watered) Edomitish סלע surrounded with precipitous rocks, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.1">Isa 16:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.42.11">Isa 42:11</reference>, the Πέτρα described by Strabo, xvi. 4, 21; the other calls to mind the Phoenician rocky island צור, <hi type="italic">Ṣûr</hi>(Tyre), the refuge in the sea.)</note> then a cleft rock, and צוּר, like the Arabic <hi type="italic">sachr</hi>, a great and hard mass of rock (Aramaic טוּר, a mountain). The figures of the מצוּדה (מצודה, מצד) and the משׂגּב are related; the former signifies properly <hi type="italic">specula</hi>, a watch-tower,<note placement="foot">In Arabic <hi type="italic">maṣâdun</hi> signifies (1) a high hill (a signification that is wanting in Freytag), (2) the summit of a mountain, and according to the original lexicons it belongs to the root Arab. <hi type="italic">maṣada</hi>, which in outward appearance is supported by the synonymous forms Arab. <hi type="italic">maṣadun</hi> and <hi type="italic">maṣdun</hi>, as also by their plurals Arab. <hi type="italic">amṣidatun</hi> and <hi type="italic">muṣdânun</hi>, wince these can only be properly formed from those singulars on the assumption of the <hi type="italic">m</hi> being part of the root. Nevertheless, since the meanings of Arab. <hi type="italic">maṣada</hi> all distinctly point to its being formed from the root Arab. <hi type="italic">mṣ</hi> contained in the reduplicated stem Arab. <hi type="italic">maṣṣa</hi>, to suck, but the meanings of Arab. <hi type="italic">maṣâdun , maṣsadun ,</hi> and <hi type="italic">maṣdun</hi> do not admit of their being referred to it, and moreover there are instances in which original <hi type="italic">nn. loci</hi> from <hi type="italic">vv. med</hi>. Arab. <hi type="italic">w</hi> and <hi type="italic">y</hi> admit of the prefixed <hi type="italic">m</hi> being treated as the first radical through forgetfulness or disregard of their derivation, and with the retention of its from secondary roots (as Arab. <hi type="italic">makana , madana , maṣṣara</hi>), it is highly probable that in <hi type="italic">maṣâd , maṣad</hi> and <hi type="italic">maṣd</hi> we have an original מצד, מצודה, מצוּדה. These Hebrew words, however, are to be referred to a צוּד in the signification to look out, therefore properly <hi type="italic">specula</hi>. - Fleischer.</note> and the latter, a steep height. The horn, which is an ancient figure of victorious and defiant power in <reference osisRef="Deut.33.17">Deu 33:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.1">1Sa 2:1</reference>, is found here applied to Jahve Himself: “horn of my salvation” is that which interposes on the side of my feebleness, conquers, and saves me. All these epithets applied to God are the fruits of the affliction out of which David’s song has sprung, viz., his persecution by Saul, when, in a country abounding in rugged rocks and deficient in forest, he betook himself to the rocks for safety, and the mountains served him as his fortresses. In the shelter which the mountains, by their natural conformations, afforded him at that time, and in the fortunate accidents, which sometimes brought him deliverance when in extreme peril, David recognises only marvellous phenomena of which Jahve Himself was to him the final cause. The confession of the God tried and known in many ways is continued in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.5">Psa 18:5</reference> by a general expression of his experience. מהלּל is a predicate accusative to יהוה: As one praised (worthy to be praised) do I call upon Jahve, - a rendering that is better suited to the following clause, which expresses confidence in the answer coinciding with the invocation, which is to be thought of as a cry for help, than Olshausen’s, “Worthy of praise, do I cry, is Jahve,” though this latter certainly is possible so far as the style is concerned (vid., on <reference osisRef="Isa.45.24">Isa 45:24</reference>, cf. also <reference osisRef="Gen.3.3">Gen 3:3</reference>; Mic 2:6). The proof of this fact, viz., that calling upon Him who is worthy to be praised, who, as the history of Israel shows, is able and willing to help, is immediately followed by actual help, as events that are coincident, forms the further matter of the Psalm.
entries.7947a0a21b52934c5d5758185404c337274173d2: <reference osisRef="Ps.18.4-Ps.18.6">Psa 18:4-6</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_18:5-7) In these verses David gathers into one collective figure all the fearful dangers to which he had been exposed during his persecution by Saul, together with the marvellous answers and deliverances he experienced, that which is unseen, which stands in the relation to that which is visible of cause and effect, rendering itself visible to him. David here appears as passive throughout; the hand from out of the clouds seizes him and draws him out of mighty waters: while in the second part of the Psalm, in fellowship with God and under His blessing, he comes forward as a free actor. <div eID="gen9208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9209" type="x-p"/> The description begins in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.5">Psa 18:5</reference> with the danger and the cry for help which is not in vain. The verb אפף according to a tradition not to be doubted (cf. אופן a wheel) signifies to go round, surround, as a poetical synonym of סבב, הקּיף, כּתּר, and not, as one might after the Arabic have thought: to drive, urge. Instead of “the bands of death,” the lxx (cf. <reference osisRef="Acts.2.24">Act 2:24</reference>) renders it ὠδῖνες (constrictive pains) θανάτου; but <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.18.6">Psa 18:6</reference></hi> favours the meaning bands, cords, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.119.61">Psa 119:61</reference> (where it is likewise חבלי instead of the הבלי, which one might have expected, <reference osisRef="Josh.17.5">Jos 17:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.36.8">Job 36:8</reference>), death is therefore represented as a hunter with a cord and net, Psa 91:3. בליּעל, compounded of בּלי and יעל (from יעל, ועל, root על), signifies unprofitableness, worthlessness, and in fact both deep-rooted moral corruption and also abysmal destruction (cf. <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.15">2Co 6:15</reference>, Βελίαρ = Βελίαλ as a name of Satan and his kingdom). Rivers of destruction are those, whose engulfing floods lead down to the abyss of destruction (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.7">Jon 2:7</reference>). Death, <hi type="italic">Belı̂jáal</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Sheôl</hi> are the names of the weird powers, which make use of David’s persecutors as their instruments. <hi type="italic">Futt</hi>. in the sense of imperfects alternate with <hi type="italic">praett</hi>. בּעת (= Arab. <hi type="italic">bgt</hi>) signifies to come suddenly upon any one (but compare also Arab. <hi type="italic">b‛ṯ</hi>, to startle, <hi type="italic">excitare</hi>, to alarm), and קדּם, to rush upon; the two words are distinguished from one another like <hi type="italic">überfallen</hi> and <hi type="italic">anfallen</hi>. The היכל out of which Jahve hears is His heavenly dwelling-place, which is both palace and temple, inasmuch as He sits enthroned there, being worshipped by blessed spirits. לפניו belongs to ושׁועתי: my cry which is poured forth before Him (as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Ps.102.1">Psa 102:1</reference>), for it is tautological if joined with תּבא beside ושׁועתי. Before Jahve’s face he made supplication and his prayer urged its way into His ears.
entries.8ff4395c703da91c0e9cdfb0be79cc07e0667cbb: <reference osisRef="Ps.18.7-Ps.18.9">Psa 18:7-9</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_18:8-10) As these verses go on to describe, the being heard became manifest in the form of deliverance. All nature stands to man in a sympathetic relationship, sharing his curse and blessing, his destruction and glory, and to God is a (so to speak) synergetic relationship, furnishing the harbingers and instruments of His mighty deeds. Accordingly in this instance Jahve’s interposition on behalf of David is accompanied by terrible manifestations in nature. Like the deliverance of Israel out of Egypt, Ps 68; Ps 77, and the giving of the Law on Sinai, Ex 19, and like the final appearing of Jahve and of Jesus Christ according to the words of prophet and apostle (Hab 3; 2Th 1:7.), the appearing of Jahve for the help of David has also extraordinary natural phenomena in its train. It is true we find no express record of any incident in David’s life of the kind recorded in <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.10">1Sa 7:10</reference>, but it must be come real experience which David here idealises (i.e., seizes at its very roots, and generalises and works up into a grand majestic picture of his miraculous deliverance). Amidst earthquake, a black thunderstorm gathers, the charging of which is heralded by the lightning’s flash, and its thick clouds descend nearer and nearer to the earth. The aorists in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.8">Psa 18:8</reference> introduce the event, for the introduction of which, from <reference osisRef="Ps.18.4">Psa 18:4</reference> onwards, the way has been prepared and towards which all is directed. The inward excitement of the Judge, who appears to His servant for his deliverance, sets the earth in violent oscillation. The foundations of the mountains (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.18">Isa 24:18</reference>) are that upon which they are supported beneath and within, as it were, the pillars which support the vast mass. געשׁ (rhyming with רעשׁ) is followed by the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. of the same verb: the first impulse having been given they, viz., the earth and the pillars of the mountains, continue to shake of themselves. These convulsions occur, because “it is kindled with respect to God;” it is unnecessary to supply אפּו, חרה לו is a synonym of חם לו. When God is wrath, according to Old Testament conception, the power of wrath which is present in Him is kindled and blazes up and breaks forth. The panting of rage may accordingly also be called the smoke of the fire of wrath (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.1">Psa 74:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.5">Psa 80:5</reference>). The smoking is as the breathing out of the fire, and the vehement hot breath which is inhaled and exhaled through the nose of one who is angry (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.41.12">Job 41:12</reference>), is like smoke rising from the internal fire of anger. The fire of anger itself “devours out of the mouth,” i.e., flames forth out of the mouth, consuming whatever it lays hold of-in men in the form of angry words, with God in the fiery forces of nature, which are of a like kind with, and subservient to, His anger, and more especially in the lightning’s flash. It is the lightning chiefly, that is compared here to the blazing up of burning coals. The power of wrath in God, becoming manifest in action, breaks forth into a glow, and before it entirely discharges its fire, it gives warning of action like the lightning’s flash heralding the outburst of the storm. Thus enraged and breathing forth His wrath, Jahve bowed the heavens, i.e., caused them to bend towards the earth, and came down, and darkness of clouds (ערפל similar in meaning to ὄρφνη, cf. ἔρεβος) was under His feet: black, low-hanging clouds announced the coming of Him who in His wrath was already on His way downwards towards the earth.
entries.7151a34eaae9a91f0444050d026eaf9255ddb2d7: <reference osisRef="Ps.18.10-Ps.18.12">Psa 18:10-12</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_18:11-13) The storm, announcing the approaching outburst of the thunderstorm, was also the forerunner of the Avenger and Deliverer. If we compare <reference osisRef="Ps.18.11">Psa 18:11</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.104.3">Psa 104:3</reference>, it is natural to regard כּרוּב as a transposition of רכוּב (a chariot, Ew. §153, <hi type="italic">a</hi>). But assuming a relationship between the biblical <hi type="italic">Cherub</hi> and (according to Ctesias) the Indo-Persian griffin, the word (from the Zend <hi type="italic">grab , garew , garefsh</hi>, to seize) signifies a creature seizing and holding irrecoverably fast whatever it seizes upon; perhaps in Semitic language the strong creature, from כּרב = Arab. <hi type="italic">krb ,</hi> <hi type="italic">torquere, constringere</hi>, whence <hi type="italic">mukrab</hi>, tight, strong). It is a passive form like גּבוּל, יסד, לבוּשׁ. The cherubim are mentioned in <reference osisRef="Gen.3.24">Gen 3:24</reference> as the guards of Paradise (this alone is enough to refute the interpretation recently revived in the <hi type="italic">Evang. Kirchen-Zeit.</hi>, 1866, No. 46, that they are a symbol of the unity of the living One, כרוב = כּרוב “like a multitude!”), and elsewhere, as it were, as the living mighty rampart and vehicle of the approach of the inaccessible majesty of God; and they are not merely in general the medium of God’s personal presence in the world, but more especially of the present of God as turning the fiery side of His doxa towards the world. As in the Prometheus of Aeschylus, Oceanus comes flying τὸν πτερυγωκῆ τόνδ ̓ οἰωνόν γνώμῃ στομίων ἄτερ εὐθύνων, so in the present passage Jahve rides upon the cherub, of which the heathenish griffin is a distortion; or, if by a comparison of passages like <reference osisRef="Ps.104.3">Psa 104:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.15">Isa 66:15</reference>, we understand David according to Ezekiel, He rides upon the cherub as upon His living throne-chariot (מרכּבה). The throne floats upon the cherubim, and this cherub-throne flies upon the wings of the wind; or, as we can also say: the cherub is the celestial spirit working in this vehicle formed of the spirit-like elements. The Manager of the chariot is Himself hidden behind the thick thunder-clouds. ישׁת is an aorist without the consecutive ו (cf. יך Hos 6:1). חשׁך is the accusative of the object to it; and the accusative of the predicate is doubled: His covering, His pavilion round about Him. In <reference osisRef="Job.36.29">Job 36:29</reference> also the thunder-clouds are called God’s סכּה, and also in <reference osisRef="Ps.97.2">Psa 97:2</reference> they are סביביו, concealing Him on all sides and announcing only His presence when He is wroth. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.18.12">Psa 18:12</reference></hi> the accusative of the object, חשׁך, is expanded into “darkness of waters,” i.e., swelling with waters<note placement="foot">Rab Dimi, <hi type="italic">B. Taanîth</hi> 10 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, for the elucidation of the passage quotes a Palestine proverb: נהור ענני זעירין מוהי חשׁוך ענני סגיין מוהי i.e., if the clouds are transparent they will yield but little water, if they are dark they will yield a quantity.</note> and billows of thick vapour, thick, and therefore dark, masses (עב in its primary meaning of denseness, or a thicket, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.9">Exo 19:9</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.4.29">Jer 4:29</reference>) of שׁחקים, which is here a poetical name for fleecy clouds. The dispersion and discharge, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.18.13">Psa 18:13</reference>, proceeded from נגהּ גגדּו. Such is the expression for the doxa of God as being a mirroring forth of His nature, as it were, over against Him, as being therefore His brightness, or the reflection of His glory. The doxa is fire and light. On this occasion the forces of wrath issue from it, and therefore it is the fiery forces: heavy and destructive hail (cf. Exo 9:23., <reference osisRef="Isa.30.30">Isa 30:30</reference>) and fiery glowing coals, i.e., flashing and kindling lightning. The object עביו stands first, because the idea of clouds, behind which, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.18.11">Psa 18:11</reference>, the doxa in concealed, is prominently connected with the doxa. It might be rendered: before His brightness His clouds turn into hail..., a rendering which would be more in accordance with the structure of the stichs, and is possible according to Ges. §138, rem. 2. Nevertheless, in connection with the combination of עבר with clouds, the idea of breaking through (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.44">Lam 3:44</reference>) is very natural. If עביו is removed, then עברו signifies “thence came forth hail...” But the mention of the clouds as the medium, is both natural and appropriate.
entries.d4bdfc0d82400195c35a77e02b7521900f2f37dd: <reference osisRef="Ps.18.13-Ps.18.15">Psa 18:13-15</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_18:14-16) Amidst thunder, Jahve hurled lightnings as arrows upon David’s enemies, and the breath of His anger laid bare the beds of the flood to the very centre of the earth, in order to rescue the sunken one. Thunder is the rumble of God, and as it were the hollow murmur of His mouth, Job 37:2. עליון, the Most High, is the name of God as the inapproachable Judge, who governs all things. The third line of <reference osisRef="Ps.18.14">Psa 18:14</reference> is erroneously repeated from the preceding strophe. It cannot be supported on grammatical grounds by <reference osisRef="Exod.9.23">Exo 9:23</reference>, since קול נתן, <hi type="italic">edere vocem</hi>, has a different meaning from the נתן קלת, <hi type="italic">dare tonitrua</hi>, of that passage. The symmetry of the strophe structure is also against it; and it is wanting both in 2 Sam. and in the lxx. רב, which, as the opposite of מעט <reference osisRef="Neh.2.12">Neh 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.7">Isa 10:7</reference>, means adverbially “in abundance,” is the parallel to ויּשׁלח. It is generally taken, after the analogy of <reference osisRef="Gen.49.23">Gen 49:23</reference>, in the sense of בּרק, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.6">Psa 144:6</reference> : רב in pause = רב (the <hi type="italic">ō</hi> passing over into the broader <hi type="italic">å</hi> like עז instead of עז in <reference osisRef="Gen.49.3">Gen 49:3</reference>) = רבב, cognate with רבה, רמה; but the forms סב, סבּוּ, here, and in every other instance, have but a very questionable existence, as e.g., רב, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.13">Isa 54:13</reference>, is more probably an adjective than the third person <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. (cf. Böttcher, <hi type="italic">Neue Aehrenlese</hi> No. 635, 1066). The suffixes <hi type="italic">ēm</hi> do not refer to the arrows, i.e., lightnings, but to David’s foes. המם means both to put in commotion and to destroy by confounding, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.24">Exo 14:24</reference>; Exo 23:27. In addition to the thunder, the voice of Jahve, comes the stormwind, which is the snorting of the breath of His nostrils. This makes the channels of the waters visible and lays bare the foundations of the earth. אפיק (collateral form to אפק) is the bed of the river and then the river or brook itself, <hi type="italic">a continendo aquas</hi> (Ges.), and exactly like the Arabic <hi type="italic">mesı̂k , mesâk ,</hi> <hi type="italic">mesek</hi>(from Arab. <hi type="italic">msk</hi>, the VI form of which, <hi type="italic">tamâsaka</hi>, corresponds to התאפּק), means a place that does not admit of the water soaking in, but on account of the firmness of the soil preserves it standing or flowing. What are here meant are the water-courses or river beds that hold the water. It is only needful for Jahve to threaten (epitiman <reference osisRef="Matt.8.26">Mat 8:26</reference>) and the floods, in which he, whose rescue is undertaken here, is sunk, flee (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.7">Psa 104:7</reference>) and dry up (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.9">Psa 106:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.4">Nah 1:4</reference>). But he is already half engulfed in the abyss of Hades, hence not merely the bed of the flood is opened up, but the earth is rent to its very centre. From the language being here so thoroughly allegorical, it is clear that we were quite correct in interpreting the description as ideal. He, who is nearly overpowered by his foes, is represented as one engulfed in deep waters and almost drowning.
entries.fc63ae89cc59c25877ba9863d94fd41746ec0c26: <reference osisRef="Ps.18.16-Ps.18.19">Psa 18:16-19</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_18:17-20) Then Jahve stretches out His hand from above into the deep chasm and draws up the sinking one. The verb שׁלח occurs also in prose (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.6">2Sa 6:6</reference>) without יד (<reference osisRef="Ps.57.4">Psa 57:4</reference>, cf. on the other hand the borrowed passage, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.7">Psa 144:7</reference>) in the signification to reach (after anything). The verb משׁה, however, is only found in one other instance, viz., <reference osisRef="Exod.2.10">Exo 2:10</reference>, as the root (transferred from the Egyptian into the Hebrew) of the name of Moses, and even Luther saw in it an historical allusion, “He hath made a Moses of me,” He hath drawn me out of great (many) waters, which had well nigh swallowed me up, as He did Moses out of the waters of the Nile, in which he would have perished. This figurative language is followed, in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.18">Psa 18:18</reference>, by its interpretation, just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.144.7">Psa 144:7</reference> the “great waters” are explained by מיּד בּני נכר, which, however, is not suitable here, or at least is too limited. <div eID="gen9209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9210" type="x-p"/> With <reference osisRef="Ps.18.17">Psa 18:17</reference> the hymn has reached the climax of epic description, from which it now descends in a tone that becomes more and more lyrical. In the combination איבי עז, עז is not an adverbial accusative, but an adjective, like רוּחך טובה <reference osisRef="Ps.143.10">Psa 143:10</reference>, and ὁ ἀνὴρ ἀγαθός (<hi type="italic">Hebräerbrief</hi> S. 353). כּי introduces the reason for the interposition of the divine omnipotence, viz., the superior strength of the foe and the weakness of the oppressed one. On the day of his איד, i.e., (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.31.12">Psa 31:12</reference>) his load or calamity, when he was altogether a homeless and almost defenceless fugitive, they came upon him (קדּם <reference osisRef="Ps.17.13">Psa 17:13</reference>), cutting off all possible means of delivering himself, but Jahve became the fugitive’s staff (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">Psa 23:4</reference>) upon which he leaned and kept himself erect. By the hand of God, out of straits and difficulties he reached a broad place, out of the dungeon of oppression to freedom, for Jahve had delighted in him, he was His chosen and beloved one. חפץ has the accent on the penult here, and <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> as a sign of the lengthening (העמדה) beside the <hi type="italic">ē</hi>, that it may not be read <hi type="italic">ĕ</hi>.<note placement="foot">In like manner <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> is placed beside the <hi type="italic">ee</hi> of the final closed syllable that has lost the tone in חפץ <reference osisRef="Ps.22.9">Psa 22:9</reference>, ותּחולל <reference osisRef="Ps.90.2">Psa 90:2</reference>, vid., <hi type="italic">Isaiah</hi> S. 594 note.</note> <div eID="gen9210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9211" type="x-p"/> The following strophe tells the reason of his pleasing God and of His not allowing him to perish. This כּי חפץ בּי (for He delighted in me) now becomes the primary thought of the song.
entries.f5f41e2e94d816195ef8159724826baa04dff759: <reference osisRef="Ps.18.20-Ps.18.23">Psa 18:20-23</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_18:21-24) On גּמל (like שׁלּם with the accusative not merely of the thing, but also of the person, e.g., <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.18">1Sa 24:18</reference>), εὐ or κακῶς πράττειν τινά, vid., on Psa 7:5. שׁמר, to observe = to keep, is used in the same way in Job 22:15. רשׁע מן is a pregnant expression of the <hi type="italic">malitiosa desertio</hi>. “From God’s side,” i.e., in His judgment, would be contrary to the general usage of the language (for the מן in <reference osisRef="Job.4.17">Job 4:17</reference> has a different meaning) and would be but a chilling addition. On the poetical form מנּי, in pause מנּי, vid., Ew. §263, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. The <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.18.23">Psa 18:23</reference></hi>, close after the substantival clause <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.18.23">Psa 18:23</reference></hi>, is not intended of the habit in the past, but at the present time: he has not wickedly forsaken God, but (כּי = <hi type="italic">imo, sed</hi>) always has God’s commandments present before him as his rule of conduct, and has not put them far away out of his sight, in order to be able to sin with less compunction; and thus then (<hi type="italic">fut. consec.</hi>) in relation (עם, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.18.13">Deu 18:13</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">2Sa 23:5</reference>) to God he was תמים, with his whole soul undividedly devoted to Him, and he guarded himself against his iniquity (עון, from עוה, Arab. <hi type="italic">'wâ</hi>, to twist, pervert, cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">gwâ</hi>, of error, delusion, self-enlightenment), i.e., not: against acquiescence in his in-dwelling sin, but: against iniquity becoming in any way his own; מעוני equivalent to מעותי (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.5">Dan 9:5</reference>), cf. מחיּי = than that I should live, Jon 4:8. In this strophe, this Psalm strikes a cord that harmonises with <reference osisRef="Ps.17.1-Ps.17.15">Psa 17:1-15</reference>, after which it is therefore placed. We may compare David’s own testimony concerning himself in 1Sa 26:23., the testimony of God in 1Ki 14:8, and the testimony of history in 1Ki 15:5; 1Ki 11:4.
entries.cf7b63735f414f8a0246750b93580d68785af06f: <reference osisRef="Ps.18.24-Ps.18.27">Psa 18:24-27</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_18:25-28) What was said in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.21">Psa 18:21</reference> is again expressed here as a result of the foregoing, and substantiated in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.26">Psa 18:26</reference>, Psa 18:27. חסיד is a friend of God and man, just as <hi type="italic">pius</hi> is used of behaviour to men as well as towards God. גּבר תמים the man (construct of גּבר) of moral and religious completeness (<hi type="italic">integri = integritatis</hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.15.2">Psa 15:2</reference>), i.e., of undivided devotion to God. נבר (instead of which we find בּר לבב elsewhere, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.4">Psa 24:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.1">Psa 73:1</reference>) not one who is purified, but, in accordance with the reflexive primary meaning of <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>., one who is purifying himself, ἁγνίζων ἑαυτόν, 1Jo 3:3. עקּשׁ (the opposite of ישׂר) one who is morally distorted, perverse. Freely formed <hi type="italic">Hithpaels</hi> are used with these attributive words to give expression to the corresponding self-manifestation: התחסּד, התּמּם (Ges. §54, 2, <hi type="italic">b</hi>), התבּרר, and התפּתּל (to show one’s self נפתּל or פּתלתּל). The fervent love of the godly man God requites with confiding love, the entire submission of the upright with a full measure of grace, the endeavour after purity by an unbeclouded charity (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.73.1">Psa 73:1</reference>), moral perverseness by paradoxical judgments, giving the perverse over to his perverseness (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.28">Rom 1:28</reference>) and leading him by strange ways to final condemnation (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.14">Isa 29:14</reference>, cf. Lev 26:23.). The truth, which is here enunciated, is not that the conception which man forms of God is the reflected image of his own mind and heart, but that God’s conduct to man is the reflection of the relation in which man has placed himself to God; cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.30">1Sa 2:30</reference>; 1Sa 15:23. This universal truth is illustrated and substantiated in Psa 18:28. The people who are bowed down by affliction experience God’s condescension, to their salvation; and their haughty oppressors, god’s exaltation, to their humiliation. Lofty, proud eyes are among the seven things that Jahve hateth, according to Pro 6:17. The judgment of God compels them to humble themselves with shame, Isa 2:11.
entries.0583156600268572ac324ca76872448939aa2a6a: <reference osisRef="Ps.18.28-Ps.18.30">Psa 18:28-30</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_18:29-31) The confirmation of what has been asserted is continued by David’s application of it to himself. Hitzig translates the futures in Psa 18:29. as imperfects; but the sequence of the tenses, which would bring this rendering with it, is in this instance interrupted, as it has been even in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.28">Psa 18:28</reference>, by כּי. The lamp, נר (contracted from <hi type="italic">nawer</hi>), is an image of life, which as it were burns on and on, including the idea of prosperity and high rank; in the form ניר (from <hi type="italic">niwr, nijr</hi>) it is the usual figurative word for the continuance of the house of David, 1Ki 11:36, and frequently. David’s life and dominion, as the covenant king, is the lamp which God’s favour has lighted for the well-being of Israel, and His power will not allow this lamp (<reference osisRef="2Sam.21.17">2Sa 21:17</reference>) to be quenched. The darkness which breaks in upon David and his house is always lighted up again by Jahve. For His strength is mighty in the weak; in, with, and by Him he can do all things. The <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. ארץ may be all the more surely derived from רצץ (= ארץ), inasmuch as this verb has the changeable <hi type="italic">u</hi> in the future also in <reference osisRef="Isa.42.4">Isa 42:4</reference>; Ecc 12:6. The text of 2 Sam 22, however, certainly seems to put “rushing upon” in the stead of “breaking down.” With <reference osisRef="Ps.18.31">Psa 18:31</reference> the first half of the hymn closes epiphonematically. האל is a <hi type="italic">nom. absol</hi>., like hatsuwr, Deu 32:4. This old Mosaic utterance is re-echoed here, as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.22">2Sa 7:22</reference>, in the mouth of David. The article of האל points to God as being manifest in past history. His way is faultless and blameless. His word is צרוּפה, not slaggy ore, but purified solid gold, Psa 12:7. Whoever retreats into Him, the God of the promise, is shielded from every danger. <reference osisRef="Prov.30.5">Pro 30:5</reference> is borrowed from this passage.
entries.78269776c1808c4101fed105843ae1b3bd8f7bbf: <reference osisRef="Ps.18.31-Ps.18.34">Psa 18:31-34</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_18:32-35) The grateful description of the tokens of favour he has experienced takes a new flight, and is continued in the second half of the Psalm in a more varied and less artificial mixture of the strophes. What is said in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.31">Psa 18:31</reference> of the way and word of Jahve and of Jahve Himself, is confirmed in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.32">Psa 18:32</reference> by the fact that He alone is אלוהּ, a divine being to be reverenced, and He alone is צוּר, a rock, i.e., a ground of confidence that cannot be shaken. What is said in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.31">Psa 18:31</reference> consequently can be said only of Him. מבּלעדי and זוּלתי alternate; the former (with a negative intensive מן) signifies “without reference to” and then absolutely “without” or besides, and the latter (with <hi type="italic">ı̂</hi> as a connecting vowel, which elsewhere has also the function of a suffix), from זוּלת (זוּלה), “exception.” The verses immediately following are attached descriptively to אלהינוּ, our God (i.e., the God of Israel), the God, who girded me with strength; and accordingly (<hi type="italic">fut. consec</hi>.) made my way תמים, “perfect,” i.e., absolutely smooth, free from stumblings and errors, leading straight forward to a divine goal. The idea is no other than that in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.31">Psa 18:31</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Job.22.3">Job 22:3</reference>, except that the freedom from error here is intended to be understood in accordance with its reference to the way of a man, of a king, and of a warrior; cf. moreover, the other text. The verb שׁוּה signifies, like Arab. <hi type="italic">swwâ</hi>, to make equal (<hi type="italic">aequare</hi>), to arrange, to set right; the dependent passage <reference osisRef="Hab.3.19">Hab 3:19</reference> has, instead of this verb, the more uncoloured שׁים. The hind, איּלה or איּלת, is the perfection of swiftness (cf. ἔλαφος and ἐλαφρός) and also of gracefulness among animals. “Like the hinds” is equivalent to like hinds’ feet; the Hebrew style leaves it to the reader to infer the appropriate point of comparison from the figure. It is not swiftness in flight (De Wette), but in attack and pursuit that is meant, - the latter being a prominent characteristic of warriors, according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.23">2Sa 1:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.18">2Sa 2:18</reference>; 1Ch 12:8. David does not call the high places of the enemy, which he has made his own by conquest “my high places,” but those heights of the Holy Land which belong to him as king of Israel: upon these Jahve preserves him a firm position, so that from them he may rule the land far and wide, and hold them victoriously (cf. passages like <reference osisRef="Deut.32.13">Deu 32:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.14">Isa 58:14</reference>). The verb למּד, which has a double accusative in other instances, is here combined with ל of the subject taught, as the aim of the teaching. The verb נחת (to press down = to bend a bow) precedes the subject “my arms” in the singular; this inequality is admissible even when the subject stands first (e.g., <reference osisRef="Gen.49.22">Gen 49:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.1.20">Joe 1:20</reference>; Zec 6:14). קשׁת נחוּשׁה a bow of brazen = of brass, as in Job 20:24. It is also the manner of heroes in Homer and in the Ramâ-jana to press down and bend with their hand a brazen bow, one end of which rests on the ground.
entries.9165b728f9151ad46ad85a2d75d4034524d3e808: <reference osisRef="Ps.18.35-Ps.18.36">Psa 18:35-36</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_18:36-37) Yet it is not the brazen bow in itself that makes him victorious, but the helpful strength of his God. “Shield of Thy salvation” is that consisting of Thy salvation. מגן has an unchangeable <hi type="italic">å</hi>, as it has always. The salvation of Jahve covered him as a shield, from which every stroke of the foe rebounded; the right hand of Jahve supported him that his hands might not become feeble in the conflict. In its ultimate cause it is the divine ענוה, to which he must trace back his greatness, i.e., God’s lowliness, by virtue of which His eyes look down upon that which is on the earth (<reference osisRef="Ps.113.6">Psa 113:6</reference>), and the poor and contrite ones are His favourite dwelling-place (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Isa 57:15</reference>; Isa 66:1.); cf. B. <hi type="italic">Megilla</hi> 31 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, “wherever Scripture testifies of the גבורה of the Holy One, blessed be He, it gives prominence also, in connection with it, to His condescension, ענותנוּתו, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.10.17">Deu 10:17</reference> and in connection with it <reference osisRef="Deut.10.18">Deu 10:18</reference>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Isa 57:15</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Isa 57:15</reference></hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.5">Psa 68:5</reference> and Psa 68:6.” The rendering of Luther, who follows the lxx and Vulgate, “When Thou humblest me, Thou makest me great” is opposed by the fact that ענוה means the bending of one’s self, and not of another. What is intended is, that condescension of God to mankind, and especially to the house of David, which was in operation, with an ultimate view to the incarnation, in the life of the son of Jesse from the time of his anointing to his death, viz., the divine χρηστότης καὶ φιλανθρωπία (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.4">Tit 3:4</reference>), which elected the shepherd boy to be king, and did not cast him off even when he fell into sin and his infirmities became manifest. To enlarge his steps under any one is equivalent to securing him room for freedom of motion (cf. the opposite form of expression in <reference osisRef="Prov.4.12">Pro 4:12</reference>). Jahve removed the obstacles of his course out of the way, and steeled his ankles so that he stood firm in fight and endured till he came off victorious. The <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. מעדו substantiates what, without any other indication of it, is required by the <hi type="italic">consecutio temporum</hi>, viz., that everything here has a retrospective meaning.
entries.d7cf997b481e6a284a6d88355d73014312bfb8ec: <reference osisRef="Ps.18.37-Ps.18.40">Psa 18:37-40</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_18:38-41) Thus in God’s strength, with the armour of God, and by God’s assistance in fight, he smote, cast down, and utterly destroyed all his foes in foreign and in civil wars. According to the Hebrew syntax the whole of this passage is a retrospect. The imperfect signification of the futures in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.38">Psa 18:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.39">Psa 18:39</reference> is made clear from the aorist which appears in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.40">Psa 18:40</reference>, and from the perfects and futures in what follows it. The strophe begins with an echo of <reference osisRef="Exod.15.9">Exo 15:9</reference> (cf. <hi type="italic">supra</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.7.6">Psa 7:6</reference>). The poet calls his opponents קמי, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.49">Psa 18:49</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.6">Psa 44:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.74.23">Psa 74:23</reference>, cf. קימנוּ <reference osisRef="Job.22.20">Job 22:20</reference>, inasmuch as קוּם by itself has the sense of rising up in hostility and consequently one can say קמי instead of עלי קמים (קומים   2Ki 16:7).<note placement="foot">In the language of the Beduins <hi type="italic">kôm</hi> is war, feud, and <hi type="italic">kômānı̂</hi> (denominative from <hi type="italic">kōm</hi>) my enemy (<hi type="italic">hostis</hi>); <hi type="italic">kōm</hi> also has the signification of a collective of <hi type="italic">kōmānı̂</hi>, and one can equally well say: <hi type="italic">entum waijânâ kôm</hi>, you and we are enemies, and: <hi type="italic">bênâtnâ kôm</hi>, there is war between us.</note> <div eID="gen9211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9212" type="x-p"/> The frequent use of this phrase (e.g., Ps 36:13, <reference osisRef="Lam.1.14">Lam 1:14</reference>) shows that קום in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.18.39">Psa 18:39</reference></hi> does not mean “to stand (resist),” but “to rise (again).” The phrase נתן ערף, however, which in other passages has those fleeing as its subject (<reference osisRef="2Chr.29.6">2Ch 29:6</reference>), is here differently applied: Thou gavest, or madest me mine enemies a back, i.e., those who turn back, as in Exo 23:27. From <reference osisRef="Ps.21.13">Psa 21:13</reference> (תּשׁיתמו שׁכם, Symm. τάξεις αὐτοὺς ἀποστρόφους) it becomes clear that ערף is not an accusative of the member beside the accusative of the person (as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Deut.33.11">Deu 33:11</reference>), but an accusative of the factitive object according to Ges. §139, 2.
entries.86d1426d4b88de7f6c2ecb897626dd9bb78df4b6: <reference osisRef="Ps.18.41-Ps.18.42">Psa 18:41-42</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_18:42-43) Their prayer to their gods, wrung from them by their distress, and even to Jahve, was in vain, because it was for their cause, and too late put up to Him. על = על; in <reference osisRef="Ps.42.2">Psa 42:2</reference> the two prepositions are interchanged. Since we do not pulverize dust but to dust, כּעפר is to be taken as describing the result: so that they became as dust (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.38.30">Job 38:30</reference>, כּאכן, so that it is become like stone, and the extreme of such pregnant brevity of expression in <reference osisRef="Isa.41.2">Isa 41:2</reference>) before the wind (על־פּני as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.3.17">2Ch 3:17</reference>, before the front). The second figure is to be explained differently: I emptied them out (אריקם from הריק) like the dirt of the streets, i.e., not merely: so that they became such, but as one empties it out, - thus contemptuously, ignominiously and completely (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">Isa 10:6</reference>; Zec 10:5). The lxx renders it λεανῶ from הרק (root רק to stretch, make thin, cf. <hi type="italic">tendo tenius, dehnen dünn</hi>); and the text of 2 Sam 22 present the same idea in אדיקם.
entries.541e0581490ec0e170a6b7abc5d6bc5aad89fca6: <reference osisRef="Ps.18.43-Ps.18.45">Psa 18:43-45</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_18:44-46) Thus victorious in God, David became what he now is, viz., the ruler of a great kingdom firmly established both in home and foreign relations. With respect to the גּוים and the verb תּפלּטני which follows, ריבי עם can only be understood of the conflicts among his own people, in which David was involved by the persecution of Saul and the rebellions of Absolom and Sheba the son of Bichri; and from which Jahve delivered him, in order to preserve him for his calling of world-wide dominion in accordance with the promise. We therefore interpret the passage according to בּרית עם in <reference osisRef="Isa.49.8">Isa 49:8</reference>, and קנאת־עם in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.11">Isa 26:11</reference>; whereas the following עם comes to have a foreign application by reason of the attributive clause לא־ידעתּי (Ges. §123, 3). The <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. נשׁמע in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.45">Psa 18:45</reference> is the reflexive of שׁמע, to obey (e.g., <reference osisRef="Exod.24.7">Exo 24:7</reference>), and is therefore to be rendered: show themselves obedient (= <hi type="italic">Ithpa</hi>. in <reference osisRef="Dan.7.27">Dan 7:27</reference>). לשׁמע אזן implies more than that they obeyed at the word; שׁמע means information, rumour, and שׁמע אזן is the opposite of personal observation (<reference osisRef="Job.42.5">Job 42:5</reference>), it is therefore to be rendered: they submitted even at the tidings of my victories; and 2Sa 8:9. is an example of this. כּחשׁ to lie, disown, feign, and flatter, is sued here, as it is frequently, of the extorted humility which the vanquished show towards the conqueror. <reference osisRef="Ps.18.46">Psa 18:46</reference> completes the picture of the reason of the sons of a foreign country “putting a good face on a bad game.” They faded away, i.e., they became weak and faint-hearted (<reference osisRef="Exod.18.18">Exo 18:18</reference>), incapable of holding out against or breaking through any siege by David, and trembled, surrendering at discretion, out of their close places, i.e., out of their strongholds behind which they had shut themselves in (cf. Ps 142:8). The signification of being alarmed, which in this instance, being found in combination with a local מן, is confined to the sense of terrified flight, is secured to the verb חרג by the Arabic <hi type="italic">ḥarija</hi> (root <hi type="italic">ḥr</hi>, of audible pressure, crowding, and the like) to be pressed, crowded, tight, or narrow, to get in a strait, and the Targumic חרנּא דמותא = אימתא דמותא (vid., the Targums on <reference osisRef="Deut.32.25">Deu 32:25</reference>). Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥjl</hi>, to limp, halt, which is compared by Hitzig, is far removed as to the sound; and the most natural, but colourless Arab. <hi type="italic">chrj</hi>, to go out of (according to its radical meaning - cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">chrq , chr‛</hi>, etc. - : to break forth, <hi type="italic">erumpere</hi>), cannot be supported in Hebrew or Aramaic. The ירגּזוּ found in the borrowed passage in Micah, Mic 7:17, favours our rendering.
entries.06129b8d32940ae09be8d869834e8a92173b874b: <reference osisRef="Ps.18.46-Ps.18.48">Psa 18:46-48</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_18:47-49) The hymn now draws towards the end with praise and thanksgiving for the multitude of God’s mighty deeds, which have just been displayed. Like the (צוּרי) בּרוּך which is always doxological, חי ה (<hi type="italic">vivus Jahve</hi>) is meant as a predicate clause, but is read with the accent of an exclamation just as in the formula of an oath, which is the same expression; and in the present instance it has a doxological meaning. Accordingly וירוּם also signifies “exalted be,” in which sense it is written וירם (וירם = וירם) in the other text. There are three doxological utterances drawn from the events which have just been celebrated in song. That which follows, from האל onwards, describes Jahve once more as the living, blessed (εὐλογητόν), and exalted One, which He has shown Himself to be. From ויּדבּר we see that הנּותן is to be resolved as an imperfect. The proofs of vengeance, נקמות, are called God’s gift, insofar as He has rendered it possible to him to punish the attacks upon his own dignity and the dignity of his people, or to witness the punishment of such insults (e.g., in the case of Nabal); for divine vengeance is a securing by punishment (<hi type="italic">vindicatio</hi>) of the inviolability of the right. It is questionable whether הדבּיר (synonym רדד, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.2">Psa 144:2</reference>) here and in <reference osisRef="Ps.47.4">Psa 47:4</reference> means “to bring to reason” as an intensive of דּבר, to drive (Ges.); the more natural meaning is “to turn the back” according to the Arabic <hi type="italic">adbara</hi> (Hitzig), cf. <hi type="italic">dabar , dabre</hi>, flight, retreat; <hi type="italic">debira</hi> to be wounded behind; <hi type="italic">medbûr</hi>, wounded in the back. The idea from which הדביר gains the meaning “to subdue” is that of flight, in which hostile nations, overtaken from behind, sank down under him (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.6">Psa 45:6</reference>); but the idea that is fully worked out in <reference osisRef="Ps.129.3">Psa 129:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.23">Isa 51:23</reference>, is by no means remote. With מפלטי the assertion takes the form of an address. מן רומם does not differ from <reference osisRef="Ps.9.14">Psa 9:14</reference> : Thou liftest me up away from mine enemies, so that I hover above them and triumph over them. The climactic אף, of which poetry is fond, here unites two thoughts of a like import to give intensity of expression to the one idea. The participle is followed by futures: his manifold experience is concentrated in one general ideal expression.
entries.c436825722baac81b62b21cd6200b61ec86ffb89: <reference osisRef="Ps.18.49-Ps.18.50">Psa 18:49-50</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_18:50-51) The praise of so blessed a God, who acts towards David as He has promised him, shall not be confined within the narrow limits of Israel. When God’s anointed makes war with the sword upon the heathen, it is, in the end, the blessing of the knowledge of Jahve for which he opens up the way, and the salvation of Jahve, which he thus mediatorially helps on. Paul has a perfect right to quote <reference osisRef="Ps.18.50">Psa 18:50</reference> of this Psalm (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.9">Rom 15:9</reference>), together with <reference osisRef="Deut.32.43">Deu 32:43</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.117.1">Psa 117:1</reference>, as proof that salvation belongs to the Gentiles also, according to the divine purpose of mercy. What is said in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.50">Psa 18:50</reference> as the reason and matter of the praise that shall go forth beyond Israel, is an echo of the Messianic promises in <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.12-2Sam.7.16">2Sa 7:12-16</reference> which is perfectly reconcileable with the Davidic authorship of the Psalm, as Hitzig acknowledges. And Theodoret does not wrongly appeal to the closing words עד־עולם against the Jews. In whom, but in Christ, the son of David, has the fallen throne of David any lasting continuance, and in whom, but in Christ, has all that has been promised to the seed of David eternal truth and reality? The praise of Jahve, the God of David, His anointed, is, according to its ultimate import, a praising of the Father of Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen9212" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Psalm 18 according to the Text of 2 Samuel 22</title> <div sID="gen9213" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.1">2Sa 22:1</reference> <div eID="gen9213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9214" type="x-p"/> On the differences of the introductory superscription, see on Psa 18:1. The relation of the prose accentuation of the Psalm in 2 Sam 22 to the poetical accentuation in the Psalter is instructive. Thus, for example, instead of <hi type="italic">Mercha mahpach</hi>. (<hi type="italic">Olewejored</hi>) in the Psalter we here find <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>; instead of the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi> following upon <hi type="italic">Mercha mahpach</hi>., here is <hi type="italic">Zakeph</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.18.7">Psa 18:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.16">Psa 18:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.31">Psa 18:31</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.7">2Sa 22:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.16">2Sa 22:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.31">2Sa 22:31</reference>); instead of <hi type="italic">Rebia mugrash,</hi> here <hi type="italic">Tiphcha</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.18.4">Psa 18:4</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.4">2Sa 22:4</reference>); instead of <hi type="italic">Pazer</hi> at the beginning of a verse, here <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.18.2">Psa 18:2</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.2">2Sa 22:2</reference>).<note placement="foot">Vid., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Accentsystem</hi> xv., and <hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi> iii. 2 together with S. 44, Anm.</note> <div eID="gen9214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9215" type="x-p"/> The peculiar mode of writing the stichs, in which we find this song in our editions, is the old traditional mode. If a half-line is placed above a half-line, so that they form two columns, it is called לבנה על־גבי לבנה אריח על־גבי אריח, brick upon brick, a half-brick upon a half-brick, as the song <hi type="italic">Haazinu</hi> in Deut 32 is set out in our editions. On the other hand if the half-lines appear as they do here divided and placed in layers one over another, it is called אריח על־גבי לבנה ולבנה על־גבי אריח. According to <hi type="italic">Megilla</hi> 16 <hi type="italic">b</hi> all the <hi type="italic">cantica</hi> in the Scriptures are to be written thus; and according to <hi type="italic">Sofrim</hi> xiii., Ps 18 has this form in common with 2 Sam 22. <div eID="gen9215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9216" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.2-2Sam.22.4">2Sa 22:2-4</reference> <div eID="gen9216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9217" type="x-p"/> This strophe is stunted by the falling away of its monostichic introit, Psa 18:2. In consequence of this, the vocatives in Psa 18:2. are deprived of their support and lowered to substantival clauses: <hi type="italic">Jahve is my Rock</hi>, etc., which form no proper beginning for a hymn. Instead of וּמפלּטי we have, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.144.2">Psa 144:2</reference>, ומפלטי־לי; and instead of אלי צוּרי we find אלהי צוּרי, which is contrary to the usual manner of arranging these emblematical names. The loss the strophe sustains is compensated by the addition: <hi type="italic">and my Refuge, my Saviour, who savest me from violence</hi>. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.22.4">2Sa 22:4</reference></hi> as in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.22.49">2Sa 22:49</reference></hi> the non-assimilated מן (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.14">2Sa 22:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.30.4">Psa 30:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.19">Psa 73:19</reference>) is shortened into an assimilated one. May לּי perhaps be the remains of the obliterated אלי, and אלהי, as it were, the clothing of the צוּרי which was then left too bare? <div eID="gen9217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9218" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.5-2Sam.22.7">2Sa 22:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen9218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9219" type="x-p"/> The connection of this strophe with the preceding by כּי accords with the sense, but is tame. On the other hand, the reading משׁבּרי instead of חבלי (even though the author of <reference osisRef="Ps.116.3">Psa 116:3</reference> may have thus read it) is commended by the parallelism, and by the fact, that now the latter figure is not repeated in <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.5">2Sa 22:5</reference>, 2Sa 22:6. משׁברי are not necessarily waves that break upon the shore, but may also be such as break one upon another, and consequently אפפוּני is not inadmissible. The ו of ונחלי, which is not wanted, is omitted. Instead of the fuller toned from סבבוּני, which is also more commensurate with the closing cadence of the verse, we have here the usual syncopated סבּוּני (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.118.11">Psa 118:11</reference>). The repetition of the אקרא (instead of אשׁוּע) is even more unpoetical than the repetition of חבלי would be. On the other hand, it might originally have been ויּשׁמע instead of ישׁמע; without ו it is an expression (intended retrospectively) of what takes place simultaneously, with ו it expresses the principal fact. The concluding line ושׁועתי בּאזניו is stunted: the brief substantival clause is not meaningless (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.15.21">Job 15:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.9">Isa 5:9</reference>), but is only a fragment of the more copious, fuller toned conclusion of the strophe which we find in the Psalter. <div eID="gen9219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9220" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.8-2Sam.22.10">2Sa 22:8-10</reference> <div eID="gen9220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9221" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> here obliterates the significant alternation of the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> and <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. of גּעשׁ. Instead of וּמוסדי we have the feminine form of the plural מוסדות (as in both texts in <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.16">2Sa 22:16</reference>) without ו. Instead of the genitive הרים, by an extension of the figure, we have השׁמים (cf. the pillars, <reference osisRef="Job.26.11">Job 26:11</reference>), which is not intended of the mountains as of Atlasses, as it were, supporting the heavens, but of the points of support and central points of the heavens themselves: the whole universe trembles. <div eID="gen9221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9222" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.11-2Sam.22.13">2Sa 22:11-13</reference> <div eID="gen9222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9223" type="x-p"/> Instead of the pictorial ויּדא (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.49">Deu 28:49</reference>, and hence in Jeremiah), which is generally used of the flight of the eagle, we have the plain, uncoloured ויּרא <hi type="italic">He appeared</hi>. Instead of ישׁת, which is intended as an aorist, we meet the more strictly regular, but here, where so many aorists with ו come together, less poetical ויּשׁת. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.22.12">2Sa 22:12</reference></hi> the rise and fall of the parallel members has grown over till it forms one heavy clumsy line: <hi type="italic">And made darkness round about Him a pavilion</hi> (סכּות). But the ἁπ. λεγ. חשׁרת, to which the signification of a “massive gathering together” is secured by the Arabic, is perhaps original.
